title: "The Developer Communication Handbook"
author: "Voytek Pitula"
date-modified: last-modified

## Intro

Communicating with people comes naturally to most of us and usually works, so we don't think about it too much. It's
also a vague and unfalsifiable topic, which is the opposite of what technical people enjoy. As a result, few of us think
about improving that skill, often to the detriment of our colleagues, teams and companies. This handbook tries to help
with that by focusing on the **parts of communication that matter to software developers**. It isn't a comprehensive
guide, and won't, for example, teach an engineering manager how to lay people off, or how to tell your kids that their
kitten has died. But it does try to teach how to:

* give and receive pull request feedback
* name and phrase things: variables, services, comments, error messages
* talk with stakeholders, managers and fellow developers (spoiler: each needs a different approach)
* share estimates and manage stakeholders' expectations
* get buy-in for unsexy work like tech-debt reduction
* disagree, deliver bad news and escalate when you're stuck
* make your work visible without boring everyone at standups
* get through job interviews and performance reviews (on either side of the table)

and much, much more, including a few general things like: how to ask questions, cross cultures, not be a (total) jerk,
and speak to a wider audience.

### Understand and adjust

There is one perfect, infallible way to communicate without any friction: **know what's inside the receiver's head and send your thoughts straight into it**.
Unfortunately, evolution never granted us that perk, so we need books like this one.

And so every piece of advice in this handbook distills down to two moves:

1. **Understand what people think.**
2. **Adjust to that.**

The whole of this book looks into different aspects of software development from those two angles: how to better
understand people we talk with and how to adjust our communication so they hear exactly what we wanted to say.

### What this book is

* **Direct.** It comes with as little sugarcoating and fluff as possible and is optimised from one perspective — developers don't
  care about communication — so everything here tries to be short, simple and directly applicable.
* **Deliberately basic.** The more experienced you are, the more obvious its content will be. Past the staff or
  engineering-manager level you're expected to read proper communication books instead.
* **Broader than the title says.** Many items are generic communication advice tailored to the developer context
  (with the generic-but-irrelevant parts cut out). It also drifts beyond communication in places — into behaviour in
  general, and sometimes into what to say rather than how to say it. That's intentional: the goal is to balance
  staying on topic with being as useful as possible.
* **Written by a developer, for remote work.** I might be biased, but I believe remote is the more common setting
  now, even for colocated teams. A lot of the advice transfers to other disciplines too, but I feel
  confident speaking only from the developer's perspective.
* **Helpful outside work.** Proper communication helps just as much with your spouse, kids or friends.

### How to read it

* **In full.** At least on the first pass. The sections cover specific scenarios, but the real goal is the intuition
  that accumulates along the way — no one can keep tens or hundreds of tiny rules in their head anyway. Once you have
  those intuitions, feel free to come back to individual sections when you want to improve a specific area. (If you won't read it in
  full, at least steal the [parting principles](#parting-principles) — the rest of the book is just them, expanded.)
* **With your brain on.** The book shows nuances and trade-offs so that you can weigh them for your particular
  situation, because it's easier to find two systems that need the same design than two conversations that need the
  same approach. It also assumes an approximate average working environment, which certainly diverges from yours
  somewhere — that's your cue to consciously ignore the advice or adjust it. And not every situation justifies the
  careful treatment described here; knowing when to let go is part of the skill.
* **As a baseline.** Communication is an art and you will end up with your own style eventually. One book won't get
  you there — there is a lot here, but expect to read [half a dozen more](#appendix-resources) to actually get good at
  this.

## Before development

Before the first line of code is written, a project exists as words alone. And words mean misunderstandings, which are
easy to create but also easy to fix. This part covers the conversations and messages that happen before coding starts.

### Extracting requirements

To deliver a product or a feature we have to know what the requirements are. The lucky among us have a product manager
or a business analyst who makes this process simpler, but even then a significant amount of work has to be put into
refining their vision. Alternatively (or in parallel), we need to talk directly with stakeholders (most of whom will be
non-technical) and figure out the requirements on our own. In either case there is a lot of talking involved and it's
important to do it effectively: extract as much _correct_ information as possible in as little time as possible
(because who likes spending time in meetings?). And do it so the other side will want to talk to us again.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People usually don’t know what solution they want, but they do know what problems they have. They
        will still ask for a solution (“add a button X”) rather than explain the problem.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make sure you understand why a feature is needed, not only what it’s supposed to do. Propose your own
        solution, but only once you know enough about the problem, otherwise you
        <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchoring_effect">anchor</a> the conversation early and risk
        solving the wrong problem.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People assume you know what’s obvious to them. So an unsaid thing is ambiguous: it may be settled, or
        never considered at all.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Confirm everything of importance. Don’t assume something has been thought through just because nobody
        flagged it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Asking many questions can feel like admitting incompetence. People stop early and start guessing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Dig until you fully understand the problem and its context, no matter how many questions it takes. A
        question costs far less than building the wrong feature.</li>
      <li>If you don’t feel like asking yet another question, share your guessed understanding and let them correct it: “so the refund
        always goes back to the original card, right?”. Confirming is easier than answering.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Business people think in terms of happy paths, and
        edge cases or errors are hard for them to consider.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Walk through concrete examples together: they confirm your understanding and flush out the edge cases
        nobody mentioned.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Non-functional requirements — performance, scalability, security — are rarely brought up by
        stakeholders on their own. Yet they drive the technical design and are your responsibility as a developer.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Raise them yourself, but in the stakeholders’ terms: how many users, how fresh the data has to be, what
        happens if it leaks.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Different stakeholders can want contradictory things, often without knowing about each other’s
        expectations.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When requirements conflict, surface the conflict back to the stakeholders instead of silently picking one
        interpretation. Resolving it in code yourself usually only makes the problem worse.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Some words have a specific meaning or are part of the jargon of a particular domain.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Start building a domain dictionary (a
        <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-driven_design">ubiquitous language</a>) early, to capture
        misunderstandings and surprising terms.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Product managers are not omniscient and might lack information.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Share any concerns you have about the project. Don’t assume the PM already knows about them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Neither the PM nor the stakeholders are responsible for the technical side of the project.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Raise technical concerns yourself, because nobody else will. Phrase them in as non-technical a way as you can.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Stakeholders (and PMs, to some extent) can’t tell how much a requirement costs to build.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Tell them the cost when it matters, since they are often keen to adjust the requirements once they see the
        price.</li>
      <li>Give a rough range with the uncertainty spelled out. A casually dropped number might get interpreted as a
        commitment (see <a href="#providing-estimates">providing estimates</a>).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Product managers are busy and often work on multiple things at once.</li>
      <li>Stakeholders have their own priorities and cannot be expected to care about the project as much as you
        do.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Propose solutions instead of asking for direction, because criticising a proposal takes far less of their
        attention than producing a starting point. (This kicks in once you understand the problem well enough — see
        the first point about anchoring.)</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You and everyone else will eventually forget things.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Write things down, whether as meeting notes or a wiki page, so that decisions and the inputs
        behind them don’t depend on anyone’s memory.</li>
      <li>Capture the decisions and the reasoning, not a transcript — nobody will read a pure meeting dump.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Providing estimates

As a software developer you will be asked for estimates constantly, whether you like it or not. It may not look like a
communication problem at first, but consider: you say "about a week", meaning the coding effort on the happy path, and
the asker hears "live in production for everyone, next Friday". The number was fine, but its meaning got lost on the
way.
A good estimate is a number that means the same thing on both sides.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People ask for estimates for many different reasons: internal planning, a public announcement, an external
        deadline (e.g. a compliance requirement), comparing work items by cost, or pricing work for a client. And sometimes
        there is no reason at all. Each calls for a different kind of answer.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If the reason isn’t clear, <em>always</em> ask why the number is needed. It’s the single most useful
        question in estimating. If no reason can be given, push back on the estimate itself.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Some reasons call for an estimate and others for a commitment, but people rarely distinguish the two words.
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Estimate</strong>: an approximation of the effort needed to deliver.</li>
          <li><strong>Commitment</strong>: a promise that something will be delivered by a certain date.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Explicitly confirm which of the two is needed. Don’t assume the asker knows the difference.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Estimates vary in scope and can include any subset of: gathering requirements, core development, automated
        tests, manual testing, deployment (to one or many environments), canary releases, monitoring, and post-release adjustments.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be explicit about what your number covers. “Done” can mean anything from “compiles on my machine” to
        “monitored in production”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Estimated time can mean two different things.
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Work-time</strong>: how much time has to be spent on the scope.</li>
          <li><strong>Calendar time</strong>: work-time adjusted for the number of people involved, their
            availability, holidays, competing projects, maintenance and unplanned fire-fighting.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say which of the two you are giving. Ten days of work can easily be a month on the calendar.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Every estimate is an approximation, and the uncertainty varies wildly. Integrating yet another data source
        into the data lake is a monthly routine, while a completely new product line is mostly guesswork.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be explicit about the uncertainty and what it does to the number. It’s completely fine to say “I’ve
        multiplied it by 1.5 because of how many open questions we still have”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The person asking usually doesn’t care about any of these details (scope, uncertainty, work-time). They
        want one number that fits their model and their context.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Numbers first, caveats later. A wall of qualifications will get skipped but can be referred to when ambiguity arises.</li>
      <li>When the uncertainty is big, a range (“3 weeks, 5 if the provider surprises us”) still leads with numbers
        without hiding the risk.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Lowering an estimate because of perceived pressure is a form of lying.
        <ul>
          <li>A correct but uncomfortably big number can start a useful negotiation, like adding people or
            cutting features.</li>
          <li>A wrong number quietly steers the project into failure.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li>If you deliver sooner than estimated, everyone is happy. If you deliver later, everyone is angry.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Underpromise and overdeliver. Don’t inflate estimates artificially, but when in doubt give the bigger
        number and adjust later.</li>
      <li>Don’t overdo the padding: work expands to fill the estimate
        (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson%27s_law">Parkinson’s law</a>), and if you always beat your
        estimates by a wide margin, people will learn to discount them. The goal is correctness, not looking good.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Estimates get more accurate as the remaining distance to the goal shrinks.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Re-estimate regularly, weekly or monthly, as unknowns get discovered and work gets completed (assuming
        anyone still needs them, which might not be the case!).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Below is an example of what an estimation message could look like.

> **Backend estimate for the payment-provider integration**
>
> * Total effort: **36 dev-days** (detailed breakdown in the linked doc)
> * Uncertainty factor: **1.3** — the domain is well known to us, but the provider is new
> * 36 × 1.3 = 47 effective dev-days
> * Each developer can dedicate 4 days a week (on-call, ops and meetings taken out)
> * Two developers assigned: 47 / 4 / 2 = **6 calendar weeks**
> * Today + 6 weeks = **23rd August**
>
> That is one week past the 15th August deadline. We will be delivering in small increments, so by the 15th
> everything except a part of the withdrawal flow should be in production. Hitting the full deadline is possible but
> not likely.
>
> The estimate covers development, testing on staging and integration with the provider's sandbox. Going to
> production might add time for non-dev activities (e.g. compliance sign-off), which we can't predict. Not included:
> spending limits and automatic conversions, both out of scope for the MVP.
>
> Usual disclaimer: the closer we get to the date, the more precise the estimate will be.

### Technical design

We write a technical design (we do, right?) to communicate our intent to build something: the vision, context and justification for the decisions taken.
In return we expect others to poke holes in it while it's still only words and cheap to change. Here we cover only the _delivery_ side of this
problem (for the _content_ you'll have to look into other resources).

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People are busy, and reviewing takes time and effort. The longer the doc, the harder it is to get a thorough
        review and an approval.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep it short, put the decision and its consequences first, and consider a ready-made template.</li>
      <li>Stay at the right abstraction level. Details make your design tangible but obscure the big picture.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Many people won’t go deep into your ideas, because they don’t have days or weeks to think about the
        topic and consider it from all angles.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If you want a thorough review, document as many of the problem’s aspects and caveats as you can. Merely
        hinting at a problem might invite a lot of comments.</li>
      <li>If your goal is approval without discussion, polish the doc as much as possible but keep it shallow. Be mindful, though, that
        this removes the safeguards and increases the risk.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s far easier for a reviewer to criticise a concrete answer than to design from a blank space.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Answer as many of the questions as you can before sharing the doc.</li>
      <li>The exception is a high-uncertainty design: share a rough draft early to check the direction before
        polishing the details.</li>
      <li>If your design still has open questions, mark them explicitly.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A design is itself a cost (in your time to write it and others’ time to review it). It’s worth paying only in
        proportion to how important the decision is and how hard it is to undo.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Scale the format to the weight of the decision: choose between a quick FYI message, a short discussion, an ADR or a
        full RFC.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Full consensus in a big group is hard to reach, because it’s hard to make everyone happy.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Consider aiming for <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7282#section-3">rough consensus</a>
        instead.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Humans are largely visual processors and comprehend images faster than text.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use a diagram to convey a high-level explanation. Add the details as prose if necessary (an
        overcomplicated image doesn’t help much).</li>
      <li>Prefer diagrams generated from text (Mermaid, PlantUML, etc.) that live next to the doc or code —
        an exported image is much harder to update.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Months or years after publishing, no one can tell if the design still reflects reality (it starts to drift
        from the code the moment it’s merged). People (should) trust a document less the older it is.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be explicit about whether it’s a snapshot or a living document. A snapshot is usually the safer choice,
        since readers already expect it to be out of date — put a date in the filename or the content so its age is
        obvious.</li>
      <li>If you do want a living document, generate it from the code wherever possible.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

See also [Getting a PR review](#getting-a-pr-review) and [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review), as some of the advice there applies to technical designs as well — including how to get the doc actually reviewed instead of published and forgotten.

### Getting buy-in

This section is a bit special, as it leans heavily on persuasion and politics and isn't really specific to
developers. Still, I've too often seen developers struggle to get approval for things like automation, tech-debt
reduction or adopting a new library or pattern. So it's here to help, and to limit the frustration and [learned
helplessness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learned_helplessness).

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A decision-maker hearing your idea for the first time in front of others might default to the safe answer, which is
        usually “no” (often disguised as “I will think about it”).</li>
      <li>People follow the crowd and agree more willingly when they see others do the same.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Present the idea in one-to-ones first and gather some backing. Either keep the decision off multi-person calls and
        use async communication instead, or use such a call only to ratify what was already agreed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The decider cares about outcomes and costs, very little about the implementation details.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on the result and why it matters to them, in their currency (e.g. bug rate, development speed,
        user experience).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Doing nothing always looks free, because that cost is hard to spot (things run on inertia).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Name the cost of inaction, e.g. the support load, slowed development or customer churn.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Doing anything carries an opportunity cost, which might be used against your proposal.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be prepared to defend your idea against alternative initiatives — not necessarily ones solving the same
        problem, but ones competing for the same resources.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The same proposal can be accepted from someone with a track record and dismissed when it comes from a
        new joiner, because the decider bets on the person as much as on the idea.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make sure you have enough credibility and social capital to cover the risks and bets in your proposal.</li>
      <li>Spend the credibility you have on the asks that matter.</li>
      <li>If you don’t feel confident enough, find a sponsor or backer who will co-own it with you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If something goes wrong, it hurts both you and the person who approved it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make the execution safe: reversible, incremental, small blast radius, cancellable. Mention this explicitly
        as an extra argument.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A big bet with a big reward is much harder to get approved than a small one with a proportionally smaller
        reward, because the risk is higher.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Instead of asking for the whole thing (e.g. a migration), ask for a spike or a prototype. If it succeeds,
        repeat until the whole thing is done.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Starting a project can take a comparable or even bigger effort than executing it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Attach the work to something already underway. “Since we’re touching this code anyway, let’s improve it a bit
        by doing X” has a much higher chance of happening than a standalone refactoring effort.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You might face a “who approved this?” question at some point.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Get the approval in writing.</li>
      <li>Scale it to the ask: for a small, reversible thing a 👍 on a Slack message is enough. Save the explicit
        sign-off for the weighty or hard-to-reverse decisions — demanding it for everything looks weird.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same pitch made in two ways.

> We should migrate off the legacy queue, the code is a mess and nobody wants to touch it.

vs.

> Migrating off the legacy queue should cut our on-call pages by about a third (most of them trace back to it) and
> speed up every checkout change we have planned for Q3. We can do it incrementally, one consumer at a time, and stop
> halfway with no harm done. And we’ll be in that code anyway for the upcoming SMS notifications.

The first asks the decider to care about your pain. The second speaks their language — fewer incidents, faster
delivery — and makes the bet safe.

## During development

This part covers the communication that happens while the features are being developed (the so-called "real work"), from
code constructs to stakeholder interactions and work visibility.

### In the code

We start with the messages that live in the code itself: comments, error messages, log lines and names. Your first
instinct might be to reject the idea that any of this belongs to communication at all, but I hope to change your mind
by the end of this section.

#### Comments

A comment is a message to someone reading your code in the future. That someone has none of your context and a
different set of knowledge and goals. That someone might as well be you in two years. So how do you write to a person
you know nothing about?

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The code already precisely encodes the logic of the program. Readable, self-explanatory code carries most of that
        weight, and AI can now help a reader decode the tricky parts.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t explain what the code does (unless you have a very good reason to do so).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People reading the code won’t have your context. They won’t know why it was written, what conversations you
        held about it, what constraints you were under, or what influenced the design.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Include everything that is relevant to the reader and can’t be recovered from the code itself.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Comments are not validated or kept in sync in any way. Anything you put in a comment that isn’t a historical
        fact will become invalid at some point, and a misleading comment wastes the reader’s time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Favour things that stay true such as “the why”, the constraints or the historical context. Treat a comment as part of
        the diff and update or delete it when the code around it changes.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The longer the comment, the more effort it takes to read and the less likely anyone reads it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep comments short and concise.</li>
      <li>Link out to external resources for the long story: wiki pages, issue trackers, internet resources.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People don’t have a tendency to revisit repos hunting for TODOs.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use a TODO to record that something was thought of but left as low priority for some <em>undefined</em>
        future. Don’t use it as a tracker for issues you actually want resolved, since there is usually no guarantee
        they will be.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A block of commented-out code is a message too, but a confusing one: is it important? Will it come back? Why was it kept?
        Am I supposed to keep it working? Meanwhile version control already remembers the old code.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Delete it. If there’s a real reason it might come back, say so in one line and link the commit or ticket
        instead.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Humans reading your code are likely to be overworked, stressed and short on patience. Or they might simply
        be having a bad day.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Drop in the occasional joke or snarky comment to make that person’s day a little better. A rant about an
        incompetent service provider can build a sense of camaraderie with the future reader — if the provider
        couldn’t deliver back then, they are unlikely to have improved since.</li>
      <li>Just keep it at nobody’s expense — with the context gone, snark aimed at a person or their code reads much
        worse than you meant it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

The general advice here is to **imagine what information might be needed by someone reading the code 5 years from now and provide it**.

Here is the same comment written in two ways.

> `// retry the request three times`

vs.

> `// The provider drops idle connections after ~30s, so the first call after a quiet period almost always fails (PAY-1421).`

The first repeats what the line below it already says. The second records the why, which is the only part a reader
can't recover from the code itself.

#### Error messages

Like a comment, an error message is a message into the future, except that the communication is about something that
didn't go well. What's worse, you can assume even less about the reader: with a comment it was most likely a developer,
while here it might be a developer, a support agent, an SRE or the user who triggered it.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A single failure might be communicated to multiple parties, all of which have different needs:
        <ul>
          <li>an on-call engineer being alerted,</li>
          <li>a developer analysing the logs,</li>
          <li>a user seeing the message in response to their action,</li>
          <li>a support agent helping that user resolve the issue,</li>
          <li>an external automated system interacting with your API,</li>
          <li>the developer using your library.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Decide who a given message is for before writing it and accommodate their needs. Using the same string for multiple things might be fine but should be done consciously.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The reader usually has some of the context that produced the error, such as a stack trace, the screen it happened on, the call being made or input values used.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t repeat what’s already available — include the things that can’t be easily accessed or
        reconstructed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The goal of an error message is either for the error to get fixed or for it not to happen again.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Give the reader enough information to act on, e.g. what failed, why, and what to do next.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>An error might need to be talked about, searched for, or quoted in a support ticket.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Consider attaching a stable error code to the message.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A user-facing error can leak information to whoever triggered it, including an adversary: “No account with
        that email” confirms which addresses are registered.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In user-facing messages, say enough to act and no more. Keep the diagnostic detail (internal IDs, the stack trace) in the logs.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same error message done in two different ways.

> Operation unsupported

vs.

> Can't update the address of an inactive user. Reactivate the account from the user's main screen first,
> then try again. [ADDR-409]

#### Logging

A log line completes the trio of messages into the future: a comment explains the code, an error explains the problem,
and a log line explains what happened.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Whoever reads the logs is likely scanning them under pressure, e.g. during an incident.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say what happened briefly and with enough context to act on it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Nobody reads logs until something breaks, and then they read a flood of lines at once. Noise hides the signal.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Log at the right level. Reserve WARN and ERROR for things a human should actually act on.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Logs are searched, filtered and grepped across millions of lines, not read like prose.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep lines greppable and consistent: stable prefixes and structured <code>key=value</code> fields rather than free text.</li>
      <li>Structured logging is even better: output the line as JSON with the fields as separate attributes, so the tooling can index and filter them instead of parsing the message. (Raw JSON is worse to read without tooling, but you can work around it when needed, e.g. with a separate renderer.)</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The logging infrastructure usually attaches data such as a timestamp, service, host or request id.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t repeat what is already there. Add what can’t be reconstructed: the why and the values
        involved.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A single request crosses many services and log streams.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Carry a correlation or request id so the lines can be stitched back together, either manually or with distributed tracing tools such as OpenTelemetry.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Logs often land somewhere with weaker access controls than the database.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Never log secrets, tokens or personal data. Log an id to correlate instead.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same event logged in two different ways.

> `ERROR Failed to send email to john.smith@gmail.com! Will retry.`

vs.

> `INFO email send failed, retry scheduled kind=weekly_digest user_id=u_1029 provider=mailgun error=connection_timeout attempt=2 max_attempts=5`

The first shouts ERROR about something that will most likely fix itself, and leaks an email address. The second is quieter, greppable, and says what happens next.

#### Naming things

A name is a small message to the person who reads the code next. It will be read far more often than written and has
to survive years or decades. And depending on the scope — a local symbol versus a whole service — it can be one of the
highest-impact messages you ever write.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A name’s scope varies a lot: from a single-line lambda, through a method, a class body, a module/namespace, a service/subsystem, up to a public API.
      The wider the scope, the more people and code depend on the name and the more costly a change to it becomes.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Scale naming effort to scope. A single letter is often enough for a lambda variable, while a public API field is worth dedicated thought.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Most names are defined inside a context, e.g. a module, package, namespace, type or class.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If a given thing (e.g. a field or method) is used mostly inside (or alongside) that context, you don’t need to repeat it — <code>user.userName</code> makes little sense.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your domain most likely already has precise words for its concepts (see
        <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-driven_design">DDD ubiquitous language</a>).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Talk with your business stakeholders and use the domain’s term rather than a personal synonym.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s normal to assume that different words mean different things.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use one term per concept — don’t mix <code>get</code>, <code>fetch</code>, <code>load</code> and <code>retrieve</code> if there is no semantic difference.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Abbreviations significantly decrease approachability and increase the learning curve of the codebase.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use abbreviations only if they are core domain terms, and don’t invent new ones for local convenience.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A reader builds a mental model based on the names and their intuition around them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Analyse how a name might be understood and whether it might be ambiguous or confusing. Assume that many people won’t read the explanation or documentation you add around the name.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The most important names get spoken aloud all the time, whenever the system is discussed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Consider how a name sounds, how it’s abbreviated and how easy it is to pronounce. Those aspects don’t change with time, and you can’t get used to them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The name of a service shapes what people assume it does and what they later try to put inside it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Name a service after its domain rather than its current purpose, so the name still fits as its responsibilities grow.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

A few names done in two ways:

* `procDt` vs `paymentProcessedAt` — the abbreviation saves a few keystrokes once and costs every reader a guess.
* `checkUser` vs `ensureUserIsActive` — “check” says neither what is checked nor what happens when the check fails.
* `getUser` / `fetchAccount` / `loadProfile` vs `getUser` / `getAccount` / `getProfile` — three different verbs
  suggest three different behaviours; if there is no difference, use one term.
* `weekly-digest-sender` vs `notifications-service` — the first stops being true the day it also sends an SMS, and by then
  the name lives in every dashboard, alert and runbook you would have to change.

### Documentation

Docs are a way to move the knowledge from your head to other people, most of whom you will never meet.
But those docs are also a liability, the same way the code is —
every documentation page has to be kept up-to-date or it turns into a trap. The art is writing as little as you can get away with, but enough to solve the real problems that arise from the lack of it.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A doc written just in case (without a real demand) will most likely never be read.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t write what nobody asked for. This applies to both standalone pages and the content within them.</li>
      <li>Yes, even onboarding guides and runbooks. The first onboarding or incident survives without them, and shows
        you exactly what’s worth writing down.</li>
      <li>The exception is external docs — there you have no access to your audience, and you will lose users faster
        than you hear about the missing page.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People don’t reach for docs by default — they ask. A question usually means the thing wasn’t obvious enough, or the doc was not obviously visible.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make the thing self-explanatory first, so no doc is needed. When you do document, keep it as close to the thing as you can — a code comment, then a package README, then docs in the repo, then the wiki, in that order.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A doc goes stale without any signal (no test failure, no build break), so first it rots and then it misleads.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Generate docs from the source whenever you can; that’s the only kind that can’t drift. Otherwise keep them next to the code and update them in the same change.</li>
      <li>Keep docs at a high enough level that they need adjusting only for big conceptual changes, not for every
        rename.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Not all docs age the same. A live doc (setup, API reference) describes how things are now and must be kept in sync forever. A snapshot (a design doc, a postmortem, a decision record) captures a moment and is never meant to change.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Know which you’re writing. A live doc is a standing liability — keep it current or kill it. A snapshot is cheap, since you never touch it again; just date it so nobody reads it as current.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People don’t read docs (or almost anything else) start to finish; they scan for the things they need.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on headings and snippets so a reader can jump straight to what they need. Prose should be minimal and reserved for actual nuance.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Code shows what and how, but the why behind a decision evaporates from the heads that made it.</li>
      <li>Code also doesn’t say <em>when</em> to reach for a given thing. A reader facing four similar methods has no
        way to tell which one their case calls for.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The why is the one thing worth writing down even when the code is clear. That’s why we have design docs, ADRs and RFCs.</li>
      <li>For anything public, document when to use it as well as what it does: which situation it’s meant for, and
        what to reach for instead when it isn’t.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Getting a PR review

Getting your code reviewed in a timely and thorough way is primarily the author's job, even though it is someone else doing the reading.
Most of it comes down to lowering the effort you ask of the people whose attention you need.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>No one likes finding obvious issues or reviewing half-baked pull requests. It signals that you didn’t value
        the reviewer’s time, and they might be slower to pick up your next request.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Do a self-review first, before passing it to other people.</li>
      <li>Make the CI green before requesting the review, or say explicitly why it’s red.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The bigger the changeset, the less likely it is to be (thoroughly) reviewed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Try to make the review as small as possible. If the work can’t be delivered (merged) in chunks, use a
        short-lived feature branch and open the smaller pull requests against it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People need context to review the changes meaningfully.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Provide an explanation of why the change is being made, e.g. in the pull request description or a Slack
        message.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Some parts of the changeset might be more important than others.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Put comments on those parts to focus the reviewer’s attention.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A review might happen at different stages of completion, e.g. before tests are written, before manual
        testing, or before some edge cases are covered. This changes how reviewers approach the
        pull request.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use a draft marker and/or put a TODO list in the description.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When a review request goes to a group, everyone assumes someone else will pick it up. This is the
        <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bystander_effect">bystander effect</a>, and the more people the request
        reaches, the stronger it gets (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffusion_of_responsibility">diffusion of
        responsibility</a>).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Ask specific people, not a group.</li>
      <li>Ask no more than two or three of them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People have a tendency to procrastinate.</li>
      <li>People have their own priorities.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Put a soft deadline or expectation on when you want the review.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>On some platforms, force-pushing destroys the incremental history and makes it impossible to review only
        what changed since the previous look.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t force-push once the pull request is public and someone might have started looking at it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A comment with no reply leaves the reviewer guessing whether you saw it, disagreed with it, or simply
        forgot.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Respond to each comment explicitly, with words or emoji.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Acknowledging a comment is not the same as satisfying it. The reviewer often wants to see <em>how</em> you
        addressed it, and sometimes to come back with more.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t resolve the reviewer’s comments yourself, unless your team has agreed otherwise. If in doubt, leave
        the formal resolution to whoever raised the comment.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A review comment lands on code you wrote, so criticism of the code is easy to take as criticism of you.
        Plain text also hides tone, which can make a blunt comment read as harsher than it was meant.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Assume good intent and read comments as being about the work. If one genuinely stings, sort it out in a
        quick call rather than in the thread.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same request for review made badly and well:

> Hey, anyone up for a review? [PR]

vs.

> \@Paolo \@Ezequiel, could you look into this PR for improved tracing in the fiat-service? I'd like to merge it by Thursday morning.

The first is addressed to nobody in particular and gives no reason to bother. The second names two people, says what
the change is for and when it needs to land.

### Providing a PR review

On the other side of the review, the roles reverse: now your comments potentially block or help someone else (or make them depressed and burnt out).
A good review catches problems (that matter) without making an enemy of the author.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Not all issues are equally important.</li>
      <li>People have finite patience for adjusting their work.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Communicate clearly on the importance of a particular issue. You can use
        <a href="https://conventionalcomments.org/">conventional comments</a>, the
        <a href="https://blog.danlew.net/2020/04/15/the-logaf-scale/">LOGAF scale</a>, or just say it in plain words.</li>
      <li>Pick your battles. Perfect is the enemy of good, so ask yourself which points are most important.</li>
      <li>Don’t block the merge on nits or taste — approve with the comments marked optional and let the author
        decide.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Some comments enforce a shared standard while others are personal taste, and the author can’t always tell
        which one they are reading.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Label taste as taste (“I’d have used a map here, but that’s me”) and let the author decide.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The author might have context you don’t, such as constraints agreed elsewhere or approaches already tried
        and abandoned. What looks like a mistake might be deliberate.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Ask before asserting: “is there a reason this isn’t X?” rather than “change this to X”. Half the time
        there is a reason.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Criticism of code is easy to take as criticism of its author.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Comment on the code, not the person: “this function swallows the error” rather than “you swallowed the
        error”.</li>
      <li>Keep the formalities and the occasional smile. They cost nothing and soften the plain text.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>“This is confusing” tells the author something is wrong but not what would satisfy you, so they have to
        guess and possibly go through another round.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Propose a solution, e.g. suggest the actual name you have in mind.</li>
      <li>For bigger issues, offer help instead of a demand, e.g. a pairing session on the fix.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The author is often blocked on your review, and a waiting pull request might accumulate merge
        conflicts.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Review quickly, or say explicitly when you’ll get to it. A decent review today is usually better than a
        thorough one in a week. Quick means prompt, not skimmed — and risky changes (migrations, money,
        security) deserve the thorough treatment.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>An objection to the whole approach costs the most when it arrives after two rounds of naming nits.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Read top-down: approach and architecture first, details later. If the approach is wrong, say so
        immediately and hold the nits. Consider a first skim on an early draft, before the effort is sunk.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Some issues predate the pull request and only became visible in the diff.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Weigh the <a href="https://deviq.com/principles/boy-scout-rule">boy scout rule</a> against the pressure
        the author is under. With no deadline in sight, asking for the cleanup is fair game, because nearby mess
        rarely gets fixed any other way. When the change is urgent, a ticket or a non-blocking comment is
        enough.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A review consisting only of flaws is demotivating, even when every flaw is real.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Point out the parts you genuinely liked. Don’t invent praise though — people can smell it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>After a few rounds of comment ping-pong, a thread stops converging and starts generating heat.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Move it to a call, then write the conclusion back into the thread so the record survives.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same review comment in two versions:

> This is wrong, don't pass a raw string here.

vs.

> **issue (blocking):** passing the raw string skips the validation that `UserId` does on construction. Could we parse it at the boundary instead? Happy to pair on it if the change spreads too far.

The first says the author is wrong and leaves them to work out why. The second explains the problem and offers a way
out, with a label that says up front how much it matters.

### Talking to non-developers

Sooner or later your work has to be explained to someone who doesn't write or even read code, like a product manager, a support agent or your grandma.
In such cases you have to become a translator from technicalese to legalese, accountinglese and other dialects that resemble English only on the surface.
(The other direction — extracting information _from_ them — is covered in [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements).)

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Non-developers don’t share your vocabulary — words like <code>PR</code>, <code>commit</code> or <code>branch</code> mean nothing to them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Drop the jargon and keep a mental list of forbidden words. Speak so your parents would understand.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Translating every term, every time, is tiring and loses nuance — and some terms are worth the whole team simply knowing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When a term keeps coming up and the distinction matters, teach it once instead of translating it forever. At some point a non-technical person might benefit from knowing what a data projection or a pull request is.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Specific terms you treat as distinct collapse into one for them: deploy, release, ship, launch all sound the same to a non-technical audience.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Spell out the distinction when it matters (a release is not a deployment), and use their coarser word when it doesn’t.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Non-devs speak imprecisely from a technical perspective — the app is “the website”, the service is “the system”. Developers speak imprecisely from a business perspective.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t correct every imprecision. Go with their words unless the difference actually matters.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Developers usually sit in one large, fairly interchangeable department, while business teams are small, specialised and often disconnected from each other. “The business” is not a single voice — two teams under the same boss can hold completely different perspectives and priorities.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t treat the business as one entity. Understand the specific teams you interact with, their responsibilities and perspectives, and don’t assume one team speaks for another or even knows what the other is doing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>They care about outcomes (what changes for them and when), not the mechanics of how the feature was built.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on impact and timing. Keep the implementation out unless someone asks.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your words might be misinterpreted and acted on — “it’s almost done” can turn into “we release on Friday”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Watch your qualifiers, be precise and make sure you’ve been understood.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>They can’t assess technical cost or risk, so they won’t notice the trade-offs on their own.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Communicate the trade-offs in business terms and let them decide.</li>
      <li>Only hand over the trade-offs that are genuinely business calls. Things like test coverage or refactoring
        are engineering calls — putting them up for a business vote is asking for trouble.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Over-explaining the details loses attention and focus.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Provide the amount of detail they need. It’s fine to under-explain and be asked for more.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Abstract technical details are received as noise, while a concrete example or an analogy is tangible and understandable.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Explain things in terms of what the user sees, or map them to something they already know.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Once in a while the non-developer is a senior manager or an executive, and you might face them without any prior experience.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t be intimidated. A good high-level manager is usually an excellent communicator, and it’s their job to bridge the gap:
      they should put you at ease, ask the right questions, and pull out what they need. Answer honestly and plainly, and let them do the steering. It feels daunting the first time, but you get used to it.</li>
      <li>Watch your casual words, though — the higher up the listener, the more weight they carry. An offhand
        “yeah, we could do that” can come back as a roadmap item.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same status update to a non-technical stakeholder in two versions:

> The PR for the idempotency keys is merged, just waiting on the migration to run in prod.

vs.

> The duplicate-charge fix is done and should be live for customers on Tuesday.

The first is accurate and means nothing to the person waiting on it. The second drops every word they'd have to translate and answers what they came for: is it fixed, and when do customers get it.

### Making your work visible

Most of your work becomes visible only when you share it. Plenty of solid engineers stay underappreciated simply because nobody sees what they do — this section is about not being one of them.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People will form an opinion of you based on the work they see, not the work you do.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If you want to be appreciated, share your progress and achievements without being asked.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Certain types of work are almost invisible to the outside world, e.g. fixing flaky tests, refactoring
        done alongside a feature, helping teammates, reviewing their work, handling support tickets, or answering
        stakeholder questions. Those usually don’t produce standalone artefacts but are no less important.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If those activities eat a significant chunk of your workday, share them like any other progress and
        achievements.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Talking about your own work feels like bragging, and the natural instinct is to stay quiet and let the
        work speak for itself. Unfortunately, the work stays silent without you. Expect the awkwardness and don’t
        wait for it to go away on its own.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Remind yourself that by posting about your work you help not only yourself but also (often primarily)
        others.</li>
      <li>Stick to facts and let the reader judge: “the import now runs in 5 minutes instead of 40, using
        incremental computation” informs and helps, while “I did an amazing job on the import” brags and is
        useless.</li>
      <li>Name the people you worked with. Taking sole credit for team work gets noticed, and not in your
        favour.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You can never know who is affected by your work or holds context you’re missing. Someone might have
        already solved the same problem, might be working on it right now, or might have learned (often the hard
        way) why it can’t be fixed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Build in the open: discuss in public channels by default and treat DMs as the exception. This increases
        the chance someone will notice and respond, even if the message is not directed at them.</li>
      <li>Some things still belong in a DM: personal feedback, security issues, anything you wouldn’t want quoted.
        Public by default, not public by dogma.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People formulate plans around your work and need to update those plans continuously.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep people in the loop and inform them about any change of schedule as soon as possible. Don’t try to
        avoid bad news.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Software development is a team sport, and the team needs to survive if you’re absent, be it due to
        holidays or career changes. A big part of your job is to make yourself replaceable.</li>
      <li>Replaceable doesn’t mean dispensable. Hoarding knowledge for job security backfires: you can’t be promoted
        away from work only you can do, and you can’t take an uninterrupted holiday from it either.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Share knowledge deliberately and continuously through demos, conversations, code reviews and any other
        means that make others familiar with what you do and help them continue that work.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People don’t like noise and will start ignoring messages that come too often or are too long.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep updates short and scannable, and make sure everything there is valuable. E.g. if you want to post
        about solving 10 different bugs last week, don’t include their details (unless some are particularly
        important).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Someone in the future might be investigating the work you did and the context around it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Leave breadcrumbs behind by linking together everything that is relevant: commits, pull requests, Jira
        tickets, Slack conversations, Confluence pages, etc.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>One day you will apply for a promotion or raise and will need to justify it. Doing it from memory alone is really hard.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep a public record of your work as you go.</li>
      <li>Read Julia Evans’ <a href="https://jvns.ca/blog/brag-documents/">post about brag documents</a> for more
        details.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

You might want to use an existing format for sharing your work. A
[5-15 report](https://swyx.io/the-importance-of-writing-weekly-updates) is a weekly update designed to take 15
minutes to write and 5 to read. Or borrow a team-wide practice like a demo Friday, or a `#shipped` channel.

## Everyday communication

The previous parts followed a project through its stages. Here we step outside that timeline and look at the
messages, pings and calls that fill every working day, whatever stage you are at. None of it is hard on its own, but
it adds up: your message is one of the hundred the receiver will see today, and small habits decide whether it lands
or gets lost.

### Asking

Asking a colleague for something looks too simple to get wrong, yet you've probably seen a question go unanswered more than once.
Your question competes with everything else in the receiver's inbox, and whether the answer arrives immediately or never is
largely decided by how the question was written. Some of the fixes below cost no more than one extra sentence.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In asynchronous communication you have to expect that every message might take minutes, hours or days to get a
        response. If you start a conversation with a single “hello” or “can I ask you about something?”, you waste
        a round-trip without providing or receiving any information.</li>
      <li>When the person you’re asking is in a distant timezone, you will see the response the next day.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Put the whole question and its context in the first message (<a href="https://nohello.net">no hello</a>,
        <a href="https://dontasktoask.com/">don’t ask to ask</a>), so the person can act without your further input.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People will usually answer the question you asked, which is not always the question you should have
        asked. If you ask about the solution you tried, they’ll help you debug it, while a far better or easier one
        might exist. This is known as the <a href="https://xyproblem.info/">XY problem</a>.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>State your goal alongside the problem you’re facing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If the person helping you doesn’t know what you’ve already tried, they’ll either suggest the same things
        or ask you about them.</li>
      <li>A question with no visible effort behind it makes responders less likely to help.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>List the things you already tried and what you found.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Asking too soon spends someone’s time on what you’d have found yourself. Struggling too long burns hours
        on something a colleague knows off-hand.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Timebox it: give it a genuine try, and once you’ve been stuck or going in circles for something like half
        an hour, ask. People remember a missed deadline or silence without progress much more than the questions you asked.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A message with several questions usually gets only some of them answered, most often just the first one.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Number your questions so it’s easy to track which ones got an answer. If the topics are separable,
        consider separate messages.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People will respond to non-targeted messages according to their availability and personal habits. Also,
        the more people are targeted, the less likely it is that any particular person will respond
        (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffusion_of_responsibility">diffusion of responsibility</a> again,
        same as with PR reviews).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li><code>@mention</code> a specific person, even if you’re not sure they’re the right one to solve your
        problem. If you pick wrongly, you will most likely be pointed in the right direction.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People are more willing to comply when given a reason, even a weak one. In
        <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Langer">Ellen Langer’s copy-machine study</a>, “may I use the
        Xerox, because I have to make copies” beat the reasonless version. (The effect faded for bigger requests
        though — a big ask deserves a real reason.)</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say why you need the thing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People are busy, and requests with no deadline are usually classified as the least urgent.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say when you need it, even roughly, e.g. “by Thursday” or “no rush, sometime this week”.</li>
      <li>Don’t inflate the urgency. If everything you send is “urgent”, your real deadlines stop being
        trusted.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same question asked in two ways:

> Hey, where can I find CPU usage metrics?

vs.

> Hey, I need to get CPU usage of our servers. Not sure who can help with this, maybe \@tiago? We are releasing a
> CPU-heavy feature on Wednesday and I need to prepare the setup.

The second names a person, states the actual goal and explains why the answer is needed by Wednesday. The first
looks cheaper to write, but it opens a slow guessing game: whoever answers doesn't know it's urgent, and "where can
I find metrics" might not even be the right question for preparing a release.


### Writing

Once you know _what_ to say, there is still the matter of _how_. The same content can get acted on immediately or postponed until never.
This section is about the form of a message: its structure, length, tone and words.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People rarely (if ever) read messages in full — most of the time they scan them. A wall of text gets postponed for
        “later”, which might never come.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make the message scannable:
        <ul>
          <li>TL;DR at the top,</li>
          <li>clearly separated paragraphs,</li>
          <li>the essence in bold,</li>
          <li>lists as bullet points.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li>Don’t overdo the formatting: if half of the message is bold, nothing gets special attention.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The reader’s attention is highest at the beginning of the message and decays fast.</li>
      <li>The first line shows up in the notification preview.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The core of the message (the ask or the key fact) should go first and the background after, so that a reader who stops
        after one line still knows what you want from them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The longer the message, the lower the chance it will be read in full.</li>
      <li>Writing short takes more effort, and when the author skips that effort, all the readers pay the
        price.</li>
      <li>“I would have written a shorter letter, but I did not have the time” (Blaise Pascal, though the internet
        prefers to credit Mark Twain).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Spend the time to trim your messages. They should be as short as possible (but not shorter).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Text carries no tone of voice, so it leaves a lot to interpretation, which is strongly influenced by the
        reader’s current mood. A neutral message can read as cold, and a hurried one as hostile.</li>
      <li>Over-enthusiasm can be worse than grumpiness — if everything is “great”, “awesome” and “incredible”, you
        lose the ability to express something exceptionally good.</li>
      <li>Readers judge how negotiable a message is by its tone. Some messages carry non-negotiable content (e.g.
        an incident that has to be handled now, or a request that was already ignored twice), and a soft tone might
        lead to expensive misunderstandings.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Aim for warm and plain: use greetings, a “thanks”, emojis and the like to properly express your
        intentions.</li>
      <li>Don’t be a pushover and don’t sugarcoat when firmness is needed. Unfortunately, figuring out the exact
        level of “firmness” is hard, and something of an art.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Strictly professional communication keeps people at arm’s length, while informality brings people
        closer. Silly emojis and memes make you “one of us”. What makes you more willing to interact with your CTO:
        the memes they post, or the official open-door policy?</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t over-sanitise your messages. Match the level of informality your team actually uses, reactions and
        dumb gifs included.</li>
      <li>Calibrate to the room. Informality that bonds one team reads as unserious in another. (Maybe it’s time to
        change teams then? Life is too short to be serious.)</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Sophisticated vocabulary adds decoding effort for every reader and makes life harder for non-native
        speakers.</li>
      <li>Words matter, and some complicated words do add clarity in the long term (especially if they are part of
        the domain). The same applies to more complicated grammar constructions.</li>
      <li>Most of the people you interact with won’t hold imperfect English against you: they are either non-native
        speakers themselves or have long since stopped noticing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Default to plain and simple words and sentences, but don’t be afraid of more complicated ones when there
        is a real benefit.</li>
      <li>Don’t be afraid of your English. Improve it if you find it subpar, but don’t let it stop you from talking
        to people.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s hard and very inconvenient to discuss two topics in a single thread.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Start a new thread for a new topic instead of hijacking an existing one.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same message written in two ways.

> Hey team, so I've been working on the invoice export for the last few days and I ran into a problem with the PDF
> library we use, it turns out it doesn't support the new layout we agreed with design, I looked into alternatives
> and there are two that could work, one is better maintained but costs money, the other is free but we'd have to
> write the table rendering ourselves, anyway I think we should decide soon because this is blocking the export
> work, let me know what you think.

vs.

> **TL;DR: the invoice export is blocked on a PDF library decision — need it by Thursday.**
>
> Our current library can't render the new layout. Two ways out:
>
> 1. **Library A** — maintained, supports everything, ~\$500/year.
> 2. **Library B** — free, but we build the table rendering ourselves (~1 week).
>
> I'd go with A unless the cost is a problem. \@Marta, your call?

The content is identical. The first has to be read whole to discover that a decision is needed; the second can be
acted on from the first line.

### Responding

A lot of communication happens after the initial message is sent: your questions need chasing, and other people's
