questions need answering. The way you handle other people's messages and responses (or the lack of them) shapes your relationships
with them.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People will forget, miss and misinterpret messages you send them. This is completely normal and shouldn’t be
        held against those people as long as it’s not pathological (i.e. it doesn’t happen with each and every message).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Repeat important messages and questions. Try to change the phrasing a bit to increase the chance
        of being understood.</li>
      <li>Give the follow-up some time to land — if you chase within an hour it reads as nagging. Unless it’s really that urgent.</li>
      <li>Try to analyse why the message could have been ignored: not clear enough? Too long? Without a clear
        recipient?</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Sending a message is just the first step, and your goal is to make sure it’s also received, understood
        and acted upon.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>For important messages ask for a confirmation and treat silence as “not received”. Don’t act like
        <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_Datagram_Protocol">UDP</a>.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your behaviour will often be mirrored by your peers.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Give the responses you want to get, even if you can’t help directly:
        <ul>
          <li>redirect to someone who might know,</li>
          <li>say “no time now, will look on Thursday”,</li>
          <li>react (a single ❌ will do) even when you have no answer, so they know the message wasn’t
            ignored.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The asker needs feedback on their message to know it was seen and that no follow-up is needed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Acknowledge what you see, either with a short message or an emoji (e.g. 👀 for “looking into it”, ✅ for
        “done”).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Every <code>@ping</code> is an interruption which can break focus, decrease productivity and annoy the
        receiver.</li>
      <li>A person pinged into a long thread has to read the whole thing to learn why they’re there.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Ping as few people as possible (but don’t hesitate to bring in people who are actually needed).</li>
      <li>When pulling someone into a long thread, give a one-line summary of what’s needed from them instead of
        “see above”. Yes, Slack can AI-summarize threads now, but it still can be you to execute that.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In a distributed team it’s hard to predict everyone’s working schedule, so the usual courtesy of “contact
        only during working hours” is hard to obey.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Send messages immediately and let the receiver manage their notifications. But don’t expect an answer
        right away.</li>
      <li>Reciprocate by muting your notifications outside your hours and don’t resent people contacting you at
        weird times.</li>
      <li>Make sure this matches the culture around you. In some teams a message from a senior person is treated as
        urgent no matter the hour, and there this approach needs an explicit agreement first.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Humans are largely driven by emotions, and emotions come and go. But the messages stay.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Never send a message under strong emotions, anger especially. Write the draft if it helps, then sit on it and delete
        it (or not) after some time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When someone asks you something, it’s tempting to answer a nearby question, or bury the answer under context. Assume they asked X for a reason.</li>
      <li>Sometimes the literal question is the wrong one — they’re asking how to do X when Y would serve them better (the <a href="#asking">XY problem</a>, now from the answering side).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Answer the actual question first and plainly, then add the caveats.</li>
      <li>If you smell an XY problem, flag it: “here’s how to do X — though if you’re after Z, Y is simpler.”</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Talking

Meetings are the most dreaded and the most expensive way to communicate — and, when done right, also the most effective
one. The trick is paying that cost only where it makes sense.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A call is costly. It demands everyone’s full attention at the same specific time (at least in theory), but
        its bandwidth is far higher than text — you can discuss much more, and more clearly, in the same amount of time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Default to asynchronous communication, but switch to a call when it’s not enough. A useful heuristic:
        make it a call if you exchanged more than 10 messages within an hour.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Sometimes the point of a call is the call itself. Especially on a remote team, a person asking for a
        meeting might be (at least partially) after human contact, not information.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t optimise every call away. Take the occasional meeting even when it’s not necessary. Build the connection and relationship.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Neither you nor anyone else will remember what you discussed after a week.</li>
      <li>There might be people who were not on the call but might be interested in the topic.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Write the conclusions back into the thread where the discussion started.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A meeting’s cost is its length multiplied by the number of participants. Take a piece of paper and calculate it for some
        slots in your calendar as an experiment.</li>
      <li>Nobody has ever complained about a meeting ending early.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep meetings as short and small as possible, and end them as soon as the goal is reached.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Meeting invitations are tricky because people can get offended when left out, and will feel obliged to join if invited.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use optional invites and share the notes afterwards, so nobody is locked out of the loop, while those whose
        presence isn’t essential feel free to skip.</li>
      <li>Don’t be afraid to decline an invitation when you don’t think you add or gain value there.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A meeting needs a stated goal for invitees to prepare and later to assess if it was successful.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Put an agenda, or at least a goal, in the meeting invitation. Repeat it at the beginning of the call.</li>
      <li>Send any materials you might have upfront. Most people won’t read them, but there is a chance someone
        will.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Meetings, especially recurring ones, often run on inertia, as nobody feels authorised to cancel
        them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Question the purpose of your meetings from time to time, and propose killing or shortening the ones that
        no longer make sense.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A very big chunk of communication is non-verbal, e.g. facial expressions or reactions.</li>
      <li>There are very few reasons to have your camera off. Eating, other people in the background — something else?</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make camera-on your strong default on calls. Don’t be afraid to ask the same from your coworkers.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A natural dynamic during a standup is to discuss an issue in detail, often taking a lot of time from
        everyone on the call, even if only a few are interested.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Once a topic exceeds a minute or two, take it after the standup with only the people involved.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Crossing cultures

Communication norms vary a lot by culture: how direct is polite, how much you say versus imply, how you treat hierarchy, what a joke or an emoji means.
On a remote, international team — which we assume in this book — you face those nuances every day, and your own defaults are just one option among many.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>What feels normal to you — how blunt, how formal, how much you spell out — is a cultural default, not a uniformly accepted baseline.</li>
      <li>Blunt feedback that feels plain-honest to you can land as an attack elsewhere. And the reverse:
        softened, indirect feedback that feels polite to you can get ignored by a colleague from a more direct
        culture.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t assume your style is the neutral one. Calibrate to the room.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>How much gets said out loud varies. A “yes” might mean “I agree” or only “I heard you”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t read a nod or a silence as agreement. Confirm what they actually mean.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Challenging a senior openly is normal in some cultures and unthinkable in others, so the same pushback lands very differently.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Learn the room’s norms before you <a href="#disagreeing-and-pushing-back">disagree</a> up the chain.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Idioms, insider jokes and emojis can be very culture-specific. Even the “same” English word can mean different things.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Inside a group that knows each other, anything goes. With a mixed audience, keep it plain and literal.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In some places trust comes from the work you deliver. In others it comes first from the relationship — a meal, some small talk, being known as a person before any business.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t always jump straight to the task. With relationship-first people, a big part of the work happens around
        it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A norm mismatch cuts both ways. When someone seems too blunt, too formal or too quiet, it’s usually their background, not rudeness — and changing ingrained habits takes time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Assume good intent, and offer a gentle hint over a cold shoulder. People adjust faster with help than with judgement.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Culture is more than nationality. Every company, team and generation (“no cap, that fit is bussin fr fr” -> “honestly, that outfit is excellent, for real”) has its own norms, so switching between any of them is a smaller version of the same problem.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Treat a new company or team as a new culture, even in your own country.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A culture is an average. “People from X are blunt” is a useful starting guess, but plenty of people break their own culture’s norms.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Treat it as a hypothesis and let the actual person correct it. Adjust to who’s in front of you, not to the
        average you started from.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

For the deeper version of all this, read *The Culture Map* (E. Meyer).

### Using AI

LLMs draft more and more of the messages, reviews and docs flying around. And it's a double-edged sword.

Caveat: this section is deliberately short and basic. We (as a civilisation) are still learning the implications of AI
and adjusting to them. Every other topic in this book has had decades to settle. AI practices change every week.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Current LLM output is verbose, generic and completely soulless. What’s worse, people are really good at detecting it.</li>
      <li>There is also the absurd loop: you inflate three bullets into three paragraphs only so that the reader can feed them back to a model to get three bullets.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t send raw output. Cut it to what you’d actually say; the model’s default length is never your message’s right length.</li>
      <li>This applies to messages, documentation, code comments and probably everything else an LLM produces for
        you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Used well, it’s a genuine help, e.g. for fixing grammar, tightening or getting past a blank page (especially for non-native speakers).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use it as an editor, not a ghostwriter. Fix and tighten, but keep your voice.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>AI will happily phrase things it doesn’t understand (if it actually understands anything in the first place), and it doesn’t have your context. The roughest words with substance are better than the smoothest without.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t outsource the thinking. You still need something to say.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Pasting an AI answer into a review or as a technical claim puts your name on something you might not be able to defend.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Only send what you understand and would stand behind yourself. “AI wrote it” is not an acceptable excuse.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Most AI output still needs a human to review it, and your AI is your responsibility. Forwarding it raw dumps your work on the reader.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Review everything yourself first. Twice.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Talking to the machine is communication too — context, a clear goal and specifics help it like they help a real person.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Brief it as clearly as you would a very competent junior.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Whatever you paste into an AI tool leaves your machine. Treat a public tool as fully public; a sanctioned enterprise one is safer (covered by an agreement) but still puts your data in a vendor’s hands.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep anything sensitive out of public tools, and know what your company’s policy allows.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>With the current spread of AI, a polished message stops signalling effort or care.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A genuine, slightly imperfect human message now stands out. Sometimes that’s the better move and can get you more credit.</li>
      <li>Raw LLM output signals the opposite — a complete lack of effort put into the phrasing. Which might be fine
        in some contexts, but not when someone actually cares.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

## Hard conversations

Sooner or later communication stops being routine and casual and starts carrying some stakes.
Such conversations are never easy, but they get much easier if you shift your perspective from "you against them" to
"it's you and them against the problem".
Let's walk through a few scenarios and see how this and other strategies help you stay out of trouble.

### Disagreeing and pushing back

Disagreement is one of the main points of communication (if everyone agrees, what's the point of talking?).
The goal, though, is not to win the discussion but to reach the better decision and _still be able to work together afterwards_.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Disagreement feels personal, but it rarely is.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on the problem and not the person: “the deadline is tight”, not “your deadline is wrong”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You might be the one missing context. The other side might have reasons you can’t see.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Ask (and understand) <em>why</em> before declaring something wrong.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People can’t weigh your opinion if they can’t tell how strongly you hold it or why.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>State your view, how sure you are, and your reasons: “I think X because Y, but it’s not a hill I’ll die on”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Pushing back on someone senior feels insubordinate (or at least intimidating), but a good manager or senior IC
      wants a plurality of opinions. Silent nodding doesn’t add any value.</li>
      <li>People can feel your disagreement even if you try to hide it and never say it out loud.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say it, politely and in private, but say it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Bringing back the same issue over and over is annoying and unhelpful, even if you’re right.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The next time you mention the problem, make sure there is some result/agreement/decision from the discussion.</li>
      <li>If the result is not what you wanted, “disagree and commit”: argue hard before the decision, then support it fully; don’t relitigate (if nothing changed) or quietly sabotage.</li>
      <li>When disagreeing, make sure you understand the other side’s perspective and the trade-offs involved.
        “We did it because we were told to” is unprofessional. “We did it because X was judged more important
        than Y” is not.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your disagreement capital is limited. If you fight everything, people will stop listening.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Pick your battles. If you have five problems, discuss the most important ones, and only one at a time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Spoken disagreements evaporate. If you’re overruled and it later goes wrong, nobody remembers the trade-off was flagged.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When it matters, put it in writing.</li>
      <li>Keep the record collaborative: write down the trade-off (“we chose X, accepting risk Y”), not an “I told
        you so” waiting to happen.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Spotting a problem is the easy half. A bare “this is broken” annoys people even if you’re right.</li>
      <li>This becomes even more important with seniority. At a certain point you are expected to be a person with
        solutions, not just problems.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You don’t always need the full fix, but bring something to the table, e.g. the problem analysis or the options you see.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same disagreement raised in two ways.

> I disagree with going multi-region now. It's premature and we'll regret it.

vs.

> I'd hold off on multi-region for now. My main worry: it roughly doubles our ops surface while we're a three-person
> team, and nothing in the current SLAs requires it, unless I'm missing something. Could we revisit once the
> enterprise deal lands? If we decide to go now anyway, I'm ok with that — but let's accept the trade-off
> explicitly.

The second states the view, the confidence and the reasoning, leaves room to be wrong, offers a way forward — and
disagrees while committing.

#### Saying no

Sometimes you will have to push back not against an idea or proposal but against a request directed at you,
like an unrealistic deadline, scope creep, or a "quick favour".

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A vague “maybe” or “I’ll try” feels polite but sets a false expectation and sabotages planning.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Give a clear answer so the person can act accordingly.</li>
      <li><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BQ4yd2W50No&amp;t=3"><em>Do. Or do not. There is no try</em></a>.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A flat “no” with no reasoning feels like a wall and invites a fight.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Explain what made you reject the request.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Every yes is a no to something else (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_cost">opportunity cost</a>) — your time and focus are finite.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Weigh a new request against what it displaces before accepting it. Use that as your justification and frame the no as a tradeoff.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Giving something is almost always better than giving nothing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Offer an alternative (“I don’t have time to investigate right now, but you can see the raw data here”) or a delay (“not now, but please ping me again tomorrow”) instead of a plain refusal.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A reflexive yes under pressure is often wrong and hard to walk back.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s fine to say “let me check and get back to you” and answer once you’ve thought it through.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Saying no upward — to your manager or lead — feels off-limits, and an outright refusal usually is.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t refuse — re-prioritise. Surface the trade-off and hand the choice back: “I can do X or Y this week,
        not both. Which one wins?”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same refusal in two ways.

> yeah I'll try to squeeze it in this week, we'll see

vs.

> I can't take this on this week without dropping the billing fix. If it can wait until Monday I'm in, otherwise you might need to ask someone else.

The first sounds nicer but helps no one (assuming you won't manage to squeeze it in). The second lets the other side make the call.

### Escalating when you're stuck

What do you do when you need to proceed but get blocked? Here we talk about situations where you need a decision or an agreement from someone else, but can't get it,
either because of lack of response or disagreement. This assumes you already asked well; if not, fix that first (see [Asking](#asking)) — a lot of blockers are just a vague request.
But sometimes a good ask isn't enough.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A polite ask buried in a thread is easy to ignore, miss or forget about.</li>
      <li>Escalating feels like (and ussually is) applying pressure, so it’s natural to sit on a blocker instead of doing something about it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Escalating is just part of the job. Do it once enough time has passed (based on the urgency of the topic) —
      in the end you’re responsible for your results and doing nothing is failing that responsibility. Just do it carefully (see below).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Escalation takes different forms with different weight. It’s usually a bad move to go straight for heavy artillery.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Raise urgency in steps:
        <ul>
          <li>a nudge: “Bumping this 🙂”</li>
          <li>a direct ask with a deadline: “Can you approve this by Thursday EOD? I’m blocked until then.”</li>
          <li>a default-decision: “Going with Postgres on Friday unless someone objects.”</li>
          <li>looping in managers: cc your manager (or theirs) on the next message, or mention it to them
            privately.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li>Match the ladder to the urgency. For a genuine emergency (production down, data at risk) skip some steps
        and escalate loudly and promptly.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Re-pinging the same “any update?” over and over is annoying and some people might ignore you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Add something with each follow-up, for example more explanation of the impact and urgency, the stakes at
        play, or the context around the request.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Decisions are costly to make, especially if they are not obvious and there are multiple things to consider.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make the decision cheap to give. Some strategies for this:
        <ul>
          <li>a recommendation: “I’d go with X, any objections?”</li>
          <li>a yes/no: turn an open question into one they can answer in a word, e.g. “Can we ship without the banner?”.</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A stalemate can persist just because nobody wants (or feels responsible enough) to be the one to decide.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use a default-decision: “I’ll do X on Friday unless someone objects.” Silence becomes a yes and you can
        move. Use it only for calls that are reasonably yours to make and that you’re willing to own.</li>
      <li>Or point at a decision-maker: instead of leaving it to the group, name who you think should call it, e.g. “@Alice, I think this is your call — can you decide by Friday?”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Escalation is about the problem. If you make it about a person, it’s called a complaint.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Raise the problem and its impact, e.g. “this is blocked and we might miss the deadline” instead of “XXX is slacking”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A private nudge is easy and polite, but it’s invisible: it leaves no record and no one else can jump in to unblock you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Start with the private nudge, but be prepared that it might not work.</li>
      <li>If it doesn’t work, move to a shared channel or ticket, keeping the problem public and the person out of it (don’t call anyone out in front of an audience).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Sometimes the person simply can’t say yes because the blocker is outside their area of influence, e.g. it’s their manager who owns priorities or budget.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In such a case, talking with the right person isn’t “going over someone’s head”. Bring that decision-maker in, ideally with the original person in the loop, not behind their back.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When the blocker is the person themselves, it starts to get tricky.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Talk to your own manager first, and try to show a pattern (a single situation is usually not worth the
        discussion). Better not to solve it yourself, unless you really know what you’re doing (but then, why are
        you reading this book?).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Escalation creates a bit of friction and might affect relations.</li>
      <li>An escalation left hanging makes people wonder if it’s still live.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Once you’re unblocked, thank whoever helped. It smooths over any friction and keeps them willing to help next time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Delivering bad news

Sooner or later you'll have to tell someone something they don't want to hear.
You can't change the past but you can change how you deliver it.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Bad news ages like milk.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Share it immediately, even if the situation is still unfolding and you don’t have the full picture yet.</li>
      <li>If you’re uncertain about the shape or impact, say so — it can reduce the panic.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People would like to know what is happening and whether the problem is being taken care of.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If you’re handling the problem, keep the audience updated. Share when they can expect the next update, e.g.
      “I should know more by the end of the day” or “I will let you know once I finish investigating” (and then actually do let them know).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Sugarcoating or burying the message doesn’t help anybody.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Start with the news, then add the details: “we’ll miss the deadline”, and only then the why.</li>
      <li>Be honest about the severity and don’t soften it into something it isn’t. Downplay the news and people
        will react to the version you gave them, not to the one you actually have.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Over-apologising makes it about your feelings and doesn’t improve the situation. At work, people care
        about the damage first and the feelings second.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on what happened, the impact and what you’re doing about it. A short “sorry” is enough.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People will be impacted by the news, e.g. a slipped deadline can wreck their plans or cause pressure from above.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Acknowledge the impact on them, e.g. “I know this messes up your timeline”. </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Hiding the problem or shifting blame costs your credibility and trust.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Take responsibility for your part, even when it’s not entirely your fault. There is no such thing as too much ownership.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Bad news might cause panic, overreaction, confusion or fear.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Consider what reaction you might get and match the channel to the news: a call or DM for the personal or highly critical, the broad channel for the broadly-impacting.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>“Here’s a disaster” with no next step is useful, but it’s only half of the story.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Bring a plan, or at least the first step towards mitigation, alongside the news.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same bad news delivered two ways.

> Hey, so I've been digging into the payment migration and there were a few complications, and I think there might be a small delay.

vs.

> Heads up: the payment migration won't hit the Tuesday deadline. A migration step failed in staging. I'm on the fix and will confirm by end of day.

Which one brings more clarity?

### Incident coordination

An incident is a special kind of bad news — one that is unfolding live, requires immediate remediation,
and usually comes with high stakes (a system, or part of it, being down; revenue or reputation being lost).
The communication around it is as important as the remediation itself, and sometimes more.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People hesitate to “raise the alarm”, e.g. for fear of overreacting, creating noise or drawing attention to themselves.</li>
      <li>Postponing the alert means postponing the fix and more downtime for the system.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When something looks wrong, confirm immediately and raise it as soon as you’re fairly confident the problem exists.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>During an incident people don’t care about the root cause — they want to know it’s being handled, what’s affected, and when it might be resolved.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Save the deep analysis for later. Focus on the status updates.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Silence during an incident creates immediate chaos — people assume nobody’s on it and start pinging
        around.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Post on a fixed cadence even when there’s nothing new, e.g. “still investigating, next update in 30 min”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People tend to follow the “room temperature” and escalate it.</li>
      <li>Panic helps no one. Being too calm can soften the reaction below the optimal point.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep the updates calm and factual, even when it’s on fire. Make urgency explicit.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s hard to debug and answer questions at the same time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If possible, split the roles: a dedicated person owns communication and coordination so the others can focus on the fix (the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incident_commander">incident-commander</a> pattern).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Coordinating a serious fix over asynchronous chat is too slow and inefficient.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Spin up a war room (get the responders onto a call to work in real time) while the comms owner keeps posting written updates to the channel for everyone else.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>During debugging it’s critical to differentiate guesses from facts — it directly affects the reasoning chain and investigation steps.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be explicit about how confident you are in each statement: “confirmed”, “likely” and “just a guess” lead
        to very different next steps.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In the middle of the firefight nobody remembers what was changed, when and why — and responders can
        collide, e.g. two people rolling back different things at once.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep a running log in the incident thread: what you observed, what you changed and when. It coordinates
        the responders now and becomes the postmortem timeline later.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s natural for multiple conversations to start about the same issue.</li>
      <li>Scattered communication makes it impossible to track the progress and the impact.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep one source of truth — a single pinned thread or status doc.</li>
      <li>Kill all other conversations explicitly with a pointer to the main one, so no one keeps answering there by accident.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People stay on edge until they’re told it’s actually over. Nobody goes back to check whether the problem
        is still live.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Mark the end explicitly — what was resolved and that normal service is back.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same incident update posted in two ways.

> guys the payments thing is still broken, we're looking at it, might be the new deploy but not sure, Marek is checking something

vs.

> **Status 14:30** — card payments failing for ~20% of users, EU only. Root cause not confirmed; rolling back the 13:50 deploy now as the most likely fix. Next update at 15:00 or sooner.

The first tells you something is broken and nothing else you can act on. The second separates facts from guesses,
states the impact and says when the next update lands.

#### Postmortems

A postmortem is a way for the organisation to learn from the incident and not repeat it.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Blame makes people hide the next incident, and fear kills the honest account you need in order to learn anything.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep it <a href="https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/">blameless</a> — describe what the system did and what people knew at the time, not who made a mistake.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The people in the room already learned most of the lesson, but most of the organisation wasn’t in the
        room.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Write it for people who didn’t participate. It’s the organisation’s memory of what happened.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Most postmortems need follow-ups (e.g. a systemic way to avoid the same problem in the future).</li>
      <li>Action items without an owner don’t get done.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Turn the lessons into action items, each with an explicitly assigned owner.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A postmortem nobody reads is wasted effort.</li>
      <li>The bad thing already happened, so sharing it costs you nothing and might save someone else the same
        outage.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Share it publicly and widely, and make it findable.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Not every incident is the same, and a postmortem is itself a cost in time and energy.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Match the effort to the severity of the issue. Sometimes a short message is enough, sometimes you will need a full report and hours of discussion.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Memory of an incident fades fast — after a few days the timeline and the small decisions are gone.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Write it soon, but not mid-adrenaline: mitigate, take a rest, then write while it’s still fresh.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

A real postmortem wouldn't fit here, so here is just the one line that decides whether the rest of it is worth writing.

> Marek deployed without running the migration check, which took payments down.

vs.

> The deploy pipeline let a schema change reach production before its migration ran. Nothing in the tooling flagged
> it, and the on-call had no way to see the mismatch.

The first is a name and a verdict, and it teaches the reader nothing except to be more careful than Marek. The second
describes a system that allowed the failure, which is the only version anyone can fix.

## Career and people

Everything so far has been about the work you do, the tasks you complete. This part is about your career and the people in it.

### Working with your manager

Conversations with your manager are the ones with the most impact on your career, and hence your life in general. Improving them even slightly can pay off for years.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The 1:1 exists primarily for you. Your manager will bring their own topics, but you can and should
        do the same.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Bring your own topics: blockers, growth, frustrations, highs, lows, and anything else you want to share.</li>
      <li>Collect topics as you go. Figuring them out on the spot rarely works.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your manager can only help with what they know, yet some developers hide problems from them — even though unblocking you is literally their job.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make sure they know. Surface problems early (see <a href="#delivering-bad-news">delivering bad news</a>).</li>
      <li>Use them. Ask for context, backing, pointers, decisions and anything else that helps you do your job better.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your manager is judged on their team, so your work and your behaviour affect them too — a mess of yours
        becomes a conversation they have to have upwards, and a win of yours is one they get to report.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Making your manager look good isn’t politics, it’s the cheapest way to buy the backing and good will
        you’ll want later.</li>
      <li>Making them look bad burns all of that.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A manager’s job is to help you grow, but they aren’t mind readers. If you never say you want to work on X or grow toward Y, you won’t.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say what you want (project, direction, money, responsibility, freedom, etc.). The worst you can hear is “not (yet)”, hopefully with some justification and context you can act on.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your manager’s manager (your “skip”) is even scarier.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t be afraid. A skip-level chat is normal and useful — just don’t use it to go around your manager.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>All of the above assumes a decent manager — and not all of them are. Some are overloaded, political or simply not on your side, and
        with those, candour can be used against you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Calibrate how much you share to the trust you’ve built. But make no mistake: a manager you have to guard
        yourself against is pathological — a signal to change teams or companies, not something you should accept.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Giving and receiving feedback

Feedback serves two purposes: to learn what you do well and to learn what can be improved. Receiving it is the easier half —
most of this section is about giving it in a way that gets heard instead of defended against. It covers feedback on people
and the way they work; feedback on code lives in [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review).

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Criticism in front of an audience is an attack on their reputation and makes people defensive. Defence is the opposite of listening.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Criticise in private.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Praise in front of others lifts the person’s standing and shows everyone what good looks like.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Praise in public whenever you can.</li>
      <li>Know your colleagues, though — some people genuinely hate the spotlight and prefer the same words in a
        DM.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Not everyone wants to hear the feedback, either in general or at a particular moment.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Ask first: “Would you like some feedback on X?”. It hands them control and primes them to listen.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Vague feedback is nearly useless. “Good job” or “be more proactive” carries only the sentiment and is
        almost impossible to act on.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Point at the specific thing and its effect. SBI (<a href="https://untools.co/situation-behavior-impact/">Situation–Behaviour–Impact</a>) is a decent template: “in yesterday’s standup (S) you cut Ana off twice (B), and she went quiet for the rest of it (I)”.</li>
      <li>This works for praise too — “your migration plan caught the rollback case” lands better than “good job”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Crediting “everyone involved” is pure noise — nobody feels seen and nobody remembers who did something nice.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Use names. Public credit is nearly free and people remember it for years.</li>
      <li>If there are many people involved, try to pick the most impactful ones or split the feedback into a couple of separate messages. If you list 20 names, it’s almost equivalent to saying “everyone”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If you save the feedback for review season, there are a few weeks or months when it couldn’t be addressed. And the memories of the exact situations have faded by then.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Give it while it’s fresh and still actionable — but not in the heat of the moment. Let the emotions
        (yours and theirs) settle first.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The only thing you know for a fact is what you observed and what you felt. You can never know what actually happened (think magic tricks) or what the people involved intended.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Offer feedback as something you noticed, and don’t try to judge the person.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Feedback aimed upward — at a senior or your manager — carries real social risk, and it’s also the feedback
        they hear least often.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Give it, but with extra care: in private, anchored to a concrete situation and its impact, and ideally
        when they’ve asked for it (many do, in 1:1s).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>On the receiving end, the instinct is to defend or explain your behaviour, which defeats the purpose (learning something).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say thanks and ask for an example.</li>
      <li>If you have something to clarify, do it a bit later, once you’ve had time to analyse what you heard.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same feedback given in two ways.

> You need to stop being so reckless with merges.

vs.

> Do you have a minute for some feedback on pull requests? The auth change on Tuesday went in about ten minutes
> after you opened it, and the question I’d left on token expiry is now live in production. I might be missing
> context on the urgency — was there a reason to ship it fast?

The first is a verdict on the person, and the only thing they can do with it is feel bad. The second asks permission,
names one situation, one behaviour and what it cost, and leaves the door open for the reason you don’t know about.

That said, some people will take the first one over the second any day — they read the careful version as padding and
would rather you just said the thing. If you know that about someone, give them the blunt one. You still need the
Tuesday and the token expiry somewhere in it, though: the brevity is negotiable but the specifics are not.

### Performance reviews

Let's now talk about that time of the year when you and your colleagues get formally evaluated on how well you did
over the last year (or half of it).
This is a form of [giving and receiving feedback](#giving-and-receiving-feedback), but with a few nuances sprinkled on top.

#### Your own

When you have to evaluate yourself and receive an evaluation from your manager.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your manager doesn’t see or remember most of what you did.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Bring it yourself, don’t assume they see what you see.</li>
      <li><a href="#making-your-work-visible">Making your work visible</a> all year removes a lot of work here — the sentiment sticks even if the details get forgotten, so there’s less to prove at review time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You won’t remember most of your accomplishments either. A year/semester/quarter is long and memory is short.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep a running log for yourself, recording anything worth remembering (achievements, deliverables,
        learning and so on).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Underselling harms your result. Inflating harms your credibility.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Stick to the facts. Emphasise things you think might be underappreciated.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Self-awareness is a skill in itself, and part of it is knowing your weak points.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be ready to name something you don’t excel at. Seriously, build a list if you have to.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>How much you grew usually matters more than how good you are — especially early in your career. At senior
        levels the bar shifts toward sustained impact.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Frame your review as a trajectory: bigger scope, new responsibilities, skills you didn’t have the last time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>“Meets expectations” is the default grade. Ratings are calibrated so most people land there by design.</li>
      <li>The bar rises with your title: higher position, higher expectations, harder to exceed.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t take a “meets” too hard. Judge it against the level you’re at.</li>
      <li>If you’re aiming to exceed, ask your manager what that would mean in practice.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You should roughly know where you stand before the review process even starts. If the result is a surprise, something went wrong during the period.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Work out why: either your manager never voiced it (their fault) or you missed the signals (a lesson on its own). Either way, fix the loop — make sure you know where you stand from your regular 1:1s.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A rating lower than you expected stings, and the instinct is to argue on the spot.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t fight it in the meeting. Ask what the rating was based on, take it away, and if you still disagree,
        come back with evidence rather than emotion.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

#### Your peers'

When you have to evaluate your colleagues and help their manager.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>360 feedback goes to the manager first, not straight to the person, so it doesn’t need the softening a
        face-to-face conversation does (though parts of it often get relayed — see the anonymity point below).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t sugarcoat it. Be blunt about the substance (but not rude in tone) — it saves your time writing and
        the manager’s time reading.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The manager has to relay your feedback, and vague input becomes something like “someone said X, but I don’t really know what they meant”.</li>
      <li>In theory they should come back to you for details, but they probably won’t. And if they do, it’s work
        you could have saved them anyway.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be specific.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A single incident doesn’t matter much, but a pattern does.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>If you notice some suboptimal behaviour in someone, look for a pattern. If you find one, keep a record of it so the specifics are easier to give.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>“Anonymous” feedback often isn’t as anonymous as you might think — content, phrasing and perspective can give you away. If only the two of you touched feature X and the feedback is about that, it becomes fairly obvious, doesn’t it?</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t count on anonymity. Write it as if they’ll know it came from you. Don’t make enemies.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your feedback has consequences. If you’re too polite, someone incompetent might get promoted. If you’re too harsh, someone might face problems they don’t deserve.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Aim to be accurate. Describe what you observed. Write only what you genuinely believe, not what you think you’re supposed to write. Integrity beats everything else.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A 360 isn’t only about problems. A specific, well-evidenced strength is often what gets a colleague
        promoted or motivated — and it’s input the manager rarely gets from anyone else.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Call out what they’re great at, with the same specificity as the criticism.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same peer feedback given in two ways.

> Marek is hard to work with.

vs.

> In the last two design reviews Marek dismissed the alternatives before they were fully explained (the queue rework and the retry design). People have stopped proposing things in his meetings.

The manager can't do anything with the first. The second names the pattern, the situations and the impact.

### Mentoring

At some point your job will be not only about you and the tasks but also about the people around you. And one aspect of that is helping them learn, sometimes through mentoring sessions.
And this activity is almost pure communication.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Asking to be mentored takes real humility (it’s not easy to say out loud that your skills are not good enough). Plenty of people never manage it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make it as easy as possible for them to get started. Run a structured programme if possible, or offer the sessions directly (it’s easier to agree than to ask for it).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Mentoring and coaching often get mixed up. Coaching is about drawing the answer out of someone without giving it (basically just asking questions). Developers usually aren’t expected to do that.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on mentoring: share what you know and what you’d do in their place. Learn more about coaching if you get interested.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When explaining things, it’s critical to know how much they know already. Assume too much understanding and they will not get the point. Assume too little and they will be offended.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make sure you know where they stand. Just ask if you’re not sure.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Most things don’t have a clear answer, and everything is a trade-off of some sort.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Instead of telling them what to do (or what you would do in their place), explain your reasoning process and the options you weigh. (You will need that skill in design interviews anyway.)</li>
      <li>When there’s time, let them attempt the problem first and then compare notes — a solution they half-built
        teaches more than one they watched. You should still share your full reasoning at the end (so you don’t drift into coaching).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>People don’t ask questions that make them feel dumb.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make it safe to ask any question. Treat a basic question as normal, and admit your own gaps when possible. Never make judgements about their level or competence.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A mentee will make communication mistakes too, like talking too much or burying the point. Most devs put
        very little thought into things like this.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Raise it directly and help them communicate better. Your sessions don’t have to be about technical topics only.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Mentoring without a goal is dangerously close to watercooler conversation.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make sure both sides agree on what the mentee actually wants to get better at, and use it as the north star for the sessions.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Almost nobody has the tenacity to keep the sessions happening. They want them to happen, but inertia and “real work” quietly win, and the sessions are missed or delayed ad infinitum.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Make it a standing slot in the calendar, so attending takes no decision and cancelling takes a bit of
        effort.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same answer to “should this call go through a queue?” in two ways.

> Yes, use a queue. That's what we do everywhere.

vs.

> What's pushing you towards one? I'd be weighing two things: whether the caller can wait for the result, and what
> should happen if the provider is down for an hour. Have a think and tell me where you land — then I'll tell you
> what I'd pick and why.

The first hands over an answer that works exactly once. The second shows the two questions that produced it, which is
the part that transfers, and it still promises the actual answer at the end so the session doesn't turn into coaching.

### Changing jobs

Job hunting is almost pure communication again, with a small twist — the thing you're selling is yourself. And when you finally land the new one it doesn't get much easier.

#### Search

The first step to landing a new job is to find interesting ones and get invited to interviews. This is what we will discuss here.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You can skip job-seeking altogether if you maintain a network of connections and relationships that can refer you to a new place.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Build relationships when working together and stay in touch once you stop. Reach out when you need a new job.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A public presence — code, articles, conference talks — can help differentiate you from other applicants and get you through the CV screening.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Do something and make it visible. The more and better things you do, the better the results.</li>
      <li>Understand the game: the payoff from public activity is slow and uncertain. Play the long game consciously and don’t expect quick returns.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The world is a small place. Recruiters might remember how you treated them.</li>
      <li><a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-red-light-district/202006/5-research-findings-concerning-karma">Karma is a thing</a>.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Even when you turn down an offer, do it with at least a basic level of decency.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your CV gets a few seconds of attention before it’s binned or kept (unless you come in as a referral).</li>
      <li>Before any human sees it, a cold application often passes through an automated keyword filter.</li>
      <li>Your CV is the channel through which you communicate with the recruiter, and there are different messages
        you might want to send:
        <ul>
          <li>deep technical expertise — familiarity with a particular tech or stack</li>
          <li>broad technical expertise — familiarity with many different stacks</li>
          <li>experience with a particular problem domain</li>
        </ul>
        And many more.
      </li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Decide which signal you want to send and make the CV carry it clearly. It has to land in the few seconds
        the CV gets.</li>
      <li>Mirror the concrete technologies from the job post (where true), so the CV survives the machine pass too.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The same signal might be relevant for multiple companies.</li>
      <li>The less focused the CV, the weaker the signal.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Life is more nuanced than “adjust your CV to a particular job”. You have to predict who is reading your CV, what signals they’re looking for, and how clear those signals are in your CV.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>“Quantify your impact” is the standard advice, but it’s a trap. Measuring things honestly (in a way that properly reflects your personal contribution to the work, and the impact that work made on the company) is horrendously hard.</li>
      <li>Any number you do use has to survive scrutiny.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be cautious about throwing numbers around — use them only when you can really defend them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Anything you put in the CV can be asked about. The more impressive, the higher the chance.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t put anything on it you can’t talk about for a couple of minutes. If you can’t defend it, remove it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

#### Interviews

Once you get invited to an interview, you start speaking to humans (hopefully). And the core struggle begins.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>In a technical interview they want to see how you think, not just the final answer.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Think out loud — narrate your reasoning and your assumptions.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>How you come across is weighed alongside what you say. Visible nerves or imposter syndrome don’t help you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Speak with confidence whatever you feel inside — leave the imposter syndrome at the door and talk like someone who knows their job. Don’t bluff though: admit what you don’t know, and own a mistake the moment you spot it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your communication skills are also judged. If you ramble or stay too abstract, it’s a problem.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Tell <em>short</em> stories: the situation, what you did, and how it turned out. Absolute minimum of details to get your point across.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A hiring loop is several people, and each is judging a different thing — a recruiter typically screens for communication and red flags, an engineer for how you work, a manager for whether you’d fit the team, a CEO for whether you move the organisation forward.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t give all of them the same pitch. Work out what each one is there to evaluate and lean into it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Software is a team sport and companies hire for it. Someone who claims they did everything alone is a red flag, regardless of their achievements.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Frame your wins as your contribution to the team’s success.</li>
      <li>But make your own part clear. “We built X” with no “I” anywhere is the other red flag — the interviewer
        needs to know what you did and decided.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The questions you ask are sometimes as important as your answers, and are being evaluated too.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Come with real questions about the team and the work you’d be doing. Good questions read as competence and genuine interest.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>“Why are you leaving?” is a trap. Trashing your current job or manager reads as a red flag about you, not them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep it forward-looking: talk about what you’re moving toward.</li>
      <li>Frame it as a tradeoff and show some understanding of the other side. Not “management is dumb” but “they optimise for things I don’t agree with”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

Here is the same answer to “tell me about a production issue you handled” in two ways.

> Oh, so, that was back when we were on the old infrastructure, we had this monolith, well, not really a monolith,
> more like two services, and one day — I think it was a Friday — alerts started firing, and my colleague was on
> holiday so I had to look at it, and the dashboards were also kind of broken at the time...

vs.

> Our payment queue started backing up during a sales peak. I traced it to a slow external call, added a timeout
> with a fallback, and we drained the backlog within the hour. Afterwards I added an alert on queue depth so we'd
> catch it earlier next time.

Same incident. The second is situation, action and result in three sentences — and it invites the interviewer to dig
exactly where they want.

#### Result

You went through the interviews and got some kind of result (good or bad). What to do now?

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Negotiating the offer feels adversarial, but by then they’ve decided they want you — you have more room than it feels like.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Treat it as a conversation, not a fight. It’s fine to ask for time instead of answering on the spot, and to let them put a number down first. For the actual tactics, read dedicated materials like <a href="https://www.kalzumeus.com/2012/01/23/salary-negotiation/">patio11's guide</a> — it’s a good one.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Telling your manager you’re leaving is not an easy conversation, and the instinct might be to soften it or dump every grievance.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Tell them directly and early. Try to keep as good a relationship as possible and don’t burn bridges.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A resignation might trigger a counteroffer.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Decide how you’d respond before you announce it. To do that, you have to really understand why you’re leaving in the first place.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your last month is the last impression you leave.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Hand over cleanly: document what’s in your head, wrap up or transfer what you can. Don’t leave a slammed door behind you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>The industry is smaller than it feels and people move around; how you take a “no” gets remembered. (For when the result is a rejection.)</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Respond to rejection gracefully, and it’s fine to ask for feedback.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

#### Onboarding

You got the job, but there are still a few things to play well.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You’re the only one who can still see what’s confusing, undocumented or weird. In a month you’ll get used to it and become blind like everyone else.</li>
      <li>The code, patterns, practices are usually “wrong” for a reason.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Write down what you notice.</li>
      <li>Learn the history and context before proposing changes. Assume the weird thing has a reason until proven otherwise.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Many things you will need aren’t written down and reside in people’s heads.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Focus on learning the company’s structure and people as much as reading code and docs, if not more.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Nobody can yet tell your silence apart from being stuck. A new joiner who goes quiet looks like struggling.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Over-communicate progress at the beginning: what you’re on, what you’ve learned, where you’re blocked.
        Scale it back once trust is established.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Interviewing candidates

Sooner or later you'll be on the other side of the table, interviewing candidates yourself — quite likely with no training, or very little of it. The golden rule here is "treat others like you would like to be treated yourself".

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>You’re evaluating the candidate, but they’re also evaluating you and the company.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s a two-way sell. Be on time, be prepared, be someone they’d want to work with. Just be a decent human being (hopefully just yourself).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A nervous candidate performs worse, and then you get a worse read on them. Your task is to evaluate how they will do on the job, so the stress level should be similar. Unless you work in a really harsh environment, the interview is not fully representative by definition.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Open warmly, explain how the session will go, and make it clear you want to see their best — not catch them out. Say it’s fine to think out loud and ask questions. Smile a lot.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s tempting to ask tricky questions and push the candidate to the limits.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s fine, but comfort them if they don’t know the answer. Make sure your question has a purpose and is not about you showing off or trying to sink the candidate.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When you talk, you don’t collect information.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Ask, then be quiet and listen. Let silences sit — people fill them with the good stuff.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>There is a chance you will form a verdict in the first couple of minutes, then spend the rest of the interview gathering evidence for it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Notice it and deliberately test the opposite. Let the candidate change your mind.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Your input feeds the hiring decision, and will be used as a baseline for the feedback given to the candidate if they ask for it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Take notes during the call and afterwards give specifics with examples — similar rules to any useful <a href="#giving-and-receiving-feedback">feedback</a>.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Sugarcoating the role or environment just to close someone might result in a disappointed hire who leaves in a few months.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Be honest about the work, the team, and the rough edges. Let them opt in with eyes open and full context.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Letting the person ask their own questions is comforting and good for the candidate.</li>
      <li>You can get quite a lot of signal from questions they ask if you look for it.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Reserve significant time for their questions.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Presenting

At some point in your career you will be forced to present something. It can be a new feature, a new idea, a knowledge sharing session or anything in between.
This section is targeted toward people who got dragged into it without any prior interest in the craft.
You won't become a keynote speaker from one handbook section, but that's not the goal.
The goal is to help you survive — and maybe even like — the internal talk you got handed. If you want to go deeper, you will find whole books on the topic in the [resources](#appendix-resources).

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>An internal audience is your colleagues, they want you to do well, and they notice far less of your mistakes than you feel.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Walk in assuming goodwill. Don’t apologise for nerves or restart — keep going.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Most talks try to say too much, and the audience leaves remembering nothing.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Pick the one thing they should walk away with. Cut whatever doesn’t serve it. Less is more.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A design review for your team and a demo for stakeholders are different talks, even about the same work.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Find out who’s in the room and what they came for, then adjust to that (see <a href="#talking-to-non-developers">talking to non-developers</a> for inspiration).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Nerves never fully go away, not even for people who do this for a living.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Prepare instead of hoping the fear passes. Rehearsals help a lot.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Slides read out word-for-word are worse than no slides; people read ahead and stop listening to you.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Keep them sparse and don’t recite. A single sentence or image per slide is the best thing you can do.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>It’s a skill, trainable like any other. Most public speakers were subpar in the beginning.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Do more of it, even if it hurts. Internal knowledge sharing sessions, local meetups, etc. Read books on the subject.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Live demos break on stage — network, environment, a flaky feature. For developers it’s one of the most
        common presentation disasters, and also the most recoverable.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Have a fallback ready (a recording, screenshots or a verbal explanation) and switch to it at the first
        failure. Never debug live in front of the room for more than a minute.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
```
