```{=html}
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Talks attract questions and interruptions, and a single side-discussion can eat half your time.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Say upfront how you’d like to take questions: on the go or at the end.</li>
      <li>“I don’t know, I’ll follow up” is a perfectly good answer, and deep dives can be deferred: “good one,
        let’s take it after the last slide”.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Communicating in public

Everything you say in the open leaves a permanent trail. The career upside of that trail is covered in
[Search](#search); this section is about the ways it can backfire.

```{=html}
<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Understand</th><th>Adjust</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>A PR comment, an issue, a Stack Overflow answer, a tweet — all of it is public, permanent, and tied to your name (even if you try to stay anonymous).</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Write it as if the person you’re talking about, and your next employer, will read it. They can. And will.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Public tech spaces reward snarky comments, hot takes and flame wars.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Don’t get pulled into that. People will be wrong on the internet, but you don’t have to correct them.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Open-source maintainers are usually unpaid volunteers who don’t owe anyone anything.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Do your best when interacting: search first, bring a reproduction, be gracious and understanding.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>Public means public — internal details, unreleased plans, or a client’s name don’t belong there.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
  <td valign="top">
    <ul>
      <li>When in doubt, keep it vague or keep it private. Nothing disappears from the internet. Be especially careful with the logs you paste.</li>
    </ul>
  </td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

## Parting principles

The whole book applies two moves — understand, then adjust — to different corners of a developer's job. One level
below sits this list: the principles behind most of the advice here. Each folds out into a few (of many) places
where the book leans on it.

### Shaping the message

- **Nobody reads in full** — people scan, losing attention as they move further from the first line. Leading with
  the point, brevity and scannable structure are all required to deliver the message.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Writing](#writing): a wall of text gets postponed for “later” — TL;DR at the top, the ask in the first line, essence in bold, so a reader who stops after the notification preview still knows what you want.
  - [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates): lead with the number (“3 weeks, 5 if the provider surprises us”) and keep the caveats for later — a wall of qualifications up front gets skipped.
  - [Delivering bad news](#delivering-bad-news): start with the news itself — “we'll miss the deadline” — and only then the why.
  - [Technical design](#technical-design): the longer the doc, the less likely a thorough review — keep it short, goal, decision and consequences first.
  - [Documentation](#documentation): nobody reads docs start to finish — build them from headings and snippets a reader can jump to.
  - [Search](#search): your CV gets a few seconds before it's binned or kept — pick clear signals and make them land within those seconds.
  :::

- **Concrete beats abstract** — examples, names, numbers, quoted phrases; vague phrasing can't be acted on and won't be
  remembered.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Giving and receiving feedback](#giving-and-receiving-feedback): “good job” and “be more proactive” carry only sentiment — point at the thing and its effect: “in yesterday's standup you cut Ana off twice, and she went quiet for the rest of it”.
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): business people think in happy paths — walking through concrete examples (“so the refund always goes back to the original card, right?”) flushes out the edge cases not mentioned before.
  - [Making your work visible](#making-your-work-visible): “the import now runs in 5 minutes instead of 40” informs; “I did an amazing job on the import” brags and is useless.
  - [Your peers'](#your-peers): “Marek is hard to work with” gives the manager nothing — “in the last two design reviews he dismissed the alternatives before they were explained” names the pattern, the situations and the impact.
  - [Talking to non-developers](#talking-to-non-developers): abstract detail lands as noise — say what the user sees: “the duplicate-charge fix should be live for customers on Tuesday”, not “the PR is merged, waiting on the migration”.
  :::

- **Explicit beats implicit** — whatever you don't spell out gets substituted with a guess. Assumptions,
  confidence, intent: say them out loud.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates): confirm whether they want an estimate or a commitment, and whether the number is work-time or calendar time — ten days of work can easily be a month on the calendar.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): separate guesses from facts out loud — “root cause not confirmed; rolling back the 13:50 deploy as the most likely fix” — because everyone's next steps depend on which is which.
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): people assume you already know what's obvious to them, so an unsaid thing may be settled or may never have been considered — confirm everything of importance.
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): the author can't tell a shared standard from your personal preference — label taste as taste: “I'd have used a map here, but that's me”.
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): state the view, the confidence and the reasons together: “I think X because Y, but it's not a hill I'll die on”.
  :::

- **Your words are not their words** — every receiver decodes with their own dictionary: the meaning of "done",
  "deliver", even "yes" varies by person. Default to clear words and teach the loaded ones.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates): you say “about a week” meaning happy-path coding and they hear “live in production next Friday” — “done” spans anything from “compiles on my machine” to “monitored in production”.
  - [Talking to non-developers](#talking-to-non-developers): deploy, release, ship and launch collapse into one word for a non-technical listener — spell out the difference when it matters, use their coarser word when it doesn't.
  - [Crossing cultures](#crossing-cultures): a “yes” might mean “I agree” or only “I heard you” — don't read a nod as agreement; confirm what they actually meant.
  - [Naming things](#naming-things): readers assume different words mean different things — `get`, `fetch` and `load` for the same behaviour suggest differences that don't exist.
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): domain words carry precise meanings you don't know yet — start a domain dictionary early to capture them.
  :::

- **Much of what you write is read in the future** — comments, logs, error messages, names, docs. That reader has none
  of your context and no way to ask, so include what can't be reconstructed.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Comments](#comments): a comment is a message to a stranger reading the code five years from now — record what can't be recovered from the code itself: the why, the constraints, the history.
  - [Error messages](#error-messages): give the future reader enough to act on — “can't update the address of an inactive user; reactivate the account first” beats “operation unsupported”.
  - [Logging](#logging): the infrastructure already stamps time, service and host — a log line should add what can't be reconstructed: the why and the values involved.
  - [Naming things](#naming-things): a name is read far more often than it's written and has to survive years of readers who won't open the docs around it.
  - [Postmortems](#postmortems): the people in the room already learned the lesson — write it for those who weren't there; it's the organisation's memory of what happened.
  - [Making your work visible](#making-your-work-visible): someone will investigate your work when you're not around to ask — leave breadcrumbs by linking the commits, tickets and conversations together.
  :::

### Reading the other side

- **Look behind the message** — think why a question is asked or a message is posted; don't take it at face value.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): stakeholders ask for a solution (“add a button X”) when what they have is a problem — dig into why the feature is needed before building what was literally requested.
  - [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates): always ask why the number is needed — planning, a public announcement and a legal deadline each call for a different answer, and no reason at all is grounds to push back.
  - [Asking](#asking), [Responding](#responding): people answer the question you asked, not the one you should have asked (the XY problem) — state your goal alongside the problem, and flag it when you smell it in someone else's question.
  - [Interviews](#interviews): “why are you leaving?” is not curiosity about your old job — it checks whether you'll trash it. Keep the answer forward-looking.
  :::

- **What looks wrong might be deliberate** — the other side can have context you can't see. Ask why before judging.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): the author may have constraints agreed elsewhere or approaches already tried — ask “is there a reason this isn't X?” rather than “change this to X”. Half the time there is a reason.
  - [Onboarding](#onboarding): in a new codebase the weird code, patterns and practices are usually “wrong” for a reason — learn the history before proposing changes.
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): you might be the one missing context — ask and understand why before declaring something wrong.
  - [Crossing cultures](#crossing-cultures): a colleague who seems too blunt or too quiet is usually following their culture's defaults, not being rude — assume good intent.
  :::

- **When you talk, you don't hear** — ask, then listen and collect information.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Interviewing candidates](#interviewing-candidates): ask, then be quiet — let the silences sit, because people fill them with the good stuff.
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): keep extracting before you propose — an early solution anchors the conversation and you risk solving the wrong problem.
  - [Giving and receiving feedback](#giving-and-receiving-feedback): on the receiving end, defending yourself defeats the point — say thanks, ask for an example, clarify later.
  :::

- **Make acting cheap** — people act when acting is easy: full context upfront, yes/no over open questions, a
  recommendation over a blank page.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Asking](#asking): put the whole question and its context in the first message — no “hello”, no “can I ask you something?” — so the receiver can act without a round-trip that might cost a day across timezones.
  - [Getting a PR review](#getting-a-pr-review): lower the reviewer's bill — small changesets, the why in the description, self-review done and CI green.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): decisions are costly to give — turn the open question into a yes/no (“can we ship without the banner?”) or attach a recommendation (“I'd go with X, any objections?”).
  :::

- **Everyone's job is no one's job** — responsibility diffuses in a crowd. Asks, decisions, action items and even
  praise need a name on them.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Getting a PR review](#getting-a-pr-review): a request to a group triggers the bystander effect, and the more people it reaches the stronger it gets — ask two or three named people.
  - [Asking](#asking): always `@mention` someone, even if you're not sure they're the right one — a wrong pick gets redirected; an untargeted message gets silence.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): a stalemate can persist just because nobody feels entitled to decide — name the decision-maker: “\@Alice, I think this is your call”.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): a dedicated, named comms owner (the incident commander) keeps the updates flowing while everyone else focuses on the fix.
  - [Postmortems](#postmortems): action items without an owner have very little chance of getting done — assign each one explicitly.
  - [Giving and receiving feedback](#giving-and-receiving-feedback): crediting “everyone involved” means nobody feels seen — praise names (and a list of 20 names is “everyone” again).
  :::

### Owning the exchange

- **You own the outcome, not just the sending** — sent doesn't mean received, received doesn't mean
  understood. Getting the answer/review/decision is your job, not just asking for it.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Getting a PR review](#getting-a-pr-review): getting code reviewed promptly and thoroughly is the author's job, even though someone else does the reading.
  - [Responding](#responding): for important messages ask for a confirmation and treat silence as “not received”.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): escalating feels like nagging, so the natural move is to sit on the blocker — but you're responsible for your results, and doing nothing is failing that responsibility.
  - [Talking to non-developers](#talking-to-non-developers): your words get acted on — “it's almost done” turns into “we release on Friday” — so make sure you've been understood, not just heard.
  :::

- **Close the loop** — silence is ambiguous, so mark the ends: conclusions into the thread, incident over, comment
  answered, thanks after unblocking.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Talking](#talking): nobody remembers what a call decided after a week — write the conclusions back into the thread where the discussion started.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): people stay on edge until told it's over — mark the end explicitly: what was resolved and that normal service is back.
  - [Responding](#responding): the asker needs to know their message was seen or they'll keep chasing — even a 👀 or ✅ closes that gap.
  - [Getting a PR review](#getting-a-pr-review): respond to each review comment explicitly, and leave the formal “resolve” to whoever raised it.
  - [Delivering bad news](#delivering-bad-news): say when the next update comes (“I should know more by end of day”) — and then actually deliver it.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): once unblocked, thank whoever helped — it marks the escalation closed and smooths the friction it created.
  :::

- **Say it early and say it straight** — discomfort tempts you to delay hard messages or dilute them, and both just
  make it pricier in the long term.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Delivering bad news](#delivering-bad-news): bad news only gets worse with time — share it immediately, even mid-investigation, and don't soften the severity: a downplayed “small delay” gets a reaction that isn't urgent enough.
  - [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates): lowering an estimate under pressure is a form of lying — the honest, uncomfortable number starts a useful negotiation, while the wrong one quietly steers the project into failure.
  - [Saying no](#saying-no): “I'll try to squeeze it in” feels polite but sets a false expectation — “I can't take this without dropping the billing fix” lets the other side act.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): people hesitate to raise the alarm for fear of overreacting, but postponing the alert postpones the fix.
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): an objection to the whole approach costs the most when it arrives after two rounds of naming nits — say it immediately and hold the small stuff.
  :::

- **Write it down** — memory fades, records don't.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): spoken disagreements evaporate — if it later goes wrong, nobody remembers the trade-off was flagged. Put “we chose X, accepting risk Y” on record, as a shared note rather than an “I told you so” in waiting.
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): everyone forgets what was agreed — capture the decisions and the reasoning, not a transcript nobody will read.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): mid-firefight nobody remembers what was changed when, and two responders can roll back different things at once — keep a running log; it becomes the postmortem timeline.
  - [Getting buy-in](#getting-buy-in): you might face “who approved this?” one day — get the approval in writing if the ask demands it.
  - [Making your work visible](#making-your-work-visible): justifying a promotion from memory alone is really hard — build a brag document as you go.
  :::

- **Communicate in the open** — easier to ignore a message than to become a telepath; DMs as the exception, not the
  norm.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Making your work visible](#making-your-work-visible): you can never know who already solved your problem, is solving it right now, or learned the hard way why it can't be solved — discuss in public channels by default, DMs as the exception.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): a private nudge is polite but invisible — when it fails, move to a shared channel, keeping the problem public and the person out of it.
  - [Postmortems](#postmortems): the bad thing already happened and sharing it can't make it worse — publish widely and make it findable.
  - [Giving and receiving feedback](#giving-and-receiving-feedback): praise in public, where it lifts the person and shows everyone what good looks like; keep criticism private.
  :::

### Conducting yourself

- **It's a [repeated game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeated_game)** — the industry is smaller than it feels and people remember. Don't be a jerk: formalities,
  conventions and smiles matter, and every review, refusal or rejection builds or spends social capital.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Getting a PR review](#getting-a-pr-review): a half-baked pull request signals you didn't value the reviewer's time — they'll be slower to pick up your next one.
  - [Communicating in public](#communicating-in-public): every public comment is permanent and tied to your name — write it as if the person you're talking about, and your next employer, will read it. They can, and will.
  - [Search](#search): recruiters remember how you treated them — turn down offers with basic decency.
  - [Result](#result): take a rejection gracefully (asking for feedback is fine) — the industry is smaller than it feels, and how you took the “no” gets remembered.
  :::

- **Control your emotions** — emotions pass but messages stay. Never send under strong emotion; draft, sit on it,
  then delete (or not).

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Responding](#responding): never send under strong emotion, anger especially — write the draft, sit on it, then delete it (or not).
  - [Performance reviews](#performance-reviews): a low rating stings, but don't fight it in the meeting — ask what it was based on, take it away, come back with evidence rather than emotion.
  - [Giving and receiving feedback](#giving-and-receiving-feedback): give feedback fresh, but never in the heat of the moment — let the emotions settle first, yours and theirs.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): people follow the room temperature and escalate it — keep updates calm and factual even when everything is on fire.
  - [Postmortems](#postmortems): don't write it mid-adrenaline — mitigate, rest, then write while it's still fresh.
  :::

- **You and them against the problem** — code not person, problem not complaint, blameless postmortems, behaviour not
  character.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): comment on the code, not the person — “this function swallows the error”, not “you swallowed the error”.
  - [Postmortems](#postmortems): blameless by design — describe what the system did and what people knew, never who made the mistake; blame makes people hide the next incident.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): escalation is about the problem; the moment it's about a person it becomes a complaint — “this is blocked and we might miss the deadline”, never “XXX is slacking”.
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): aim at the problem — “the deadline is tight”, not “your deadline is wrong”.
  :::

- **Bring something to the table** — criticising is far cheaper than creating, so come with options, an analysis or a
  plan next to every problem. Use the asymmetry in both directions.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Extracting requirements](#extracting-requirements): once you understand the problem, propose solutions instead of asking for direction — criticising a proposal takes far less of a busy PM's attention than producing one.
  - [Technical design](#technical-design): reviewers criticise a concrete answer far more easily than they design from blank space — answer the open questions before sharing, or the gaps come back as vague comments.
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): a bare “this is broken” annoys people even when you're right — bring the analysis or the options you see.
  - [Delivering bad news](#delivering-bad-news): “here's a disaster” is half the story — bring a plan, or at least the first step towards mitigation.
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): “this is confusing” forces the author to guess — suggest the actual name you have in mind, or offer a pairing session for the bigger fixes.
  :::

- **Guard your credibility** — it's a budget: honesty and integrity refill it slowly, while inflated urgency, padded
  estimates and unbacked numbers spend it fast. Framing still matters.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Asking](#asking): don't inflate urgency — if everything you send is “urgent”, your real deadlines stop being trusted.
  - [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates): don't overdo the padding — always beating your estimates by a wide margin teaches people to discount them.
  - [Performance reviews](#performance-reviews): underselling harms your result, inflating harms your credibility — stick to facts you can defend.
  - [Search](#search): “quantify your impact” is a trap unless the number survives scrutiny — remove from your CV anything you can't talk about for a couple of minutes.
  - [Getting buy-in](#getting-buy-in): the decider bets on you as much as on the idea — spend your credibility on the asks that matter, and find a sponsor when you're short.
  :::

### Spending wisely

- **Communication is hard and costly** — not always worth the effort. Scale it to the stakes.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Technical design](#technical-design): scale the format to how important and hard to undo the decision is — a quick FYI, a discussion, an ADR or a full RFC.
  - [Documentation](#documentation): every doc is a liability that has to be kept current or it turns into a trap — write as little as you can get away with, and skip the pages nobody asked for.
  - [Naming things](#naming-things): a single letter is fine for a lambda variable, while a public API field will be read for years and deserves dedicated thought.
  - [Postmortems](#postmortems): match the effort to the severity — sometimes a short message, sometimes a full report and hours of discussion.
  - [Getting buy-in](#getting-buy-in): a 👍 on Slack covers a small reversible change; save the formal sign-off for the weighty ones — demanding it for everything looks weird.
  :::

- **Text is cheap, talk is powerful** — switch to a call when text stops converging, then write the outcome back to
  where the discussion started.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Talking](#talking): default to async, but once you've exchanged more than ten messages in an hour, make it a call.
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): after a few rounds of comment ping-pong a thread stops converging and starts generating heat — move to a call, then write the conclusion back so the record survives.
  - [Incident coordination](#incident-coordination): chat is too slow for a serious fix — spin up a war room, while a comms owner keeps posting written updates for everyone else.
  :::

- **Pick your battles and let go** — disagreement capital is limited; five problems usually means discussing the most
  important one, not all five.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): disagreement capital is limited — if you fight everything, people stop listening.
  - [Providing a PR review](#providing-a-pr-review): don't block the merge on nits or taste — approve with the comments marked optional and let the author decide.
  - [Disagreeing and pushing back](#disagreeing-and-pushing-back): when the decision goes against you, disagree and commit — argue hard before, support it fully after, no relitigating and no quiet sabotage.
  - [Talking to non-developers](#talking-to-non-developers): the app is “the website” and the service is “the system” — don't correct every imprecision; go with their words unless the difference matters.
  - [Communicating in public](#communicating-in-public): people will be wrong on the internet — you don't have to correct them.
  :::

- **Consult your manager** — the universal escape hatch. Whatever the mess (a conflict, a blocker, politics), helping
  you through it is literally their job.

  ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true" icon="false" title="Examples"}
  - [Working with your manager](#working-with-your-manager): some developers hide problems from the one person whose literal job is unblocking them — surface problems early and ask for context, backing, decisions.
  - [Escalating when you're stuck](#escalating-when-youre-stuck): when the blocker is a person rather than a decision, go to your manager first, with a pattern of situations — don't try to fix a person yourself.
  - [Saying no](#saying-no): an outright refusal upward is usually off-limits — re-prioritise instead: “I can do X or Y this week, not both. Which one wins?”
  - [Performance reviews](#performance-reviews): a rating that surprises you means the feedback loop broke months earlier — fix it so your 1:1s always tell you where you stand.
  :::

## Outro

One caveat before you go. This whole book was about packaging: how to shape a message, whom to aim it at, when to
send it. And that packaging is not optional, but it's also not enough. **At the end of the day you have to have something to say**,
and no amount of technique will hide it if you don't.

The other thing worth saying: this skill compounds. The estimate that was believed, the review that didn't
make an enemy, the escalation that worked — none of them look like much on their own, but stack a few years of them
and people start noticing. They might not know what they notice exactly, but the way you're perceived changes. And that's something that
can push your career forward when you've already achieved technical mastery.

There is still no way to know what's inside the receiver's head. Until evolution ships that update, understand, adjust, repeat.

## Appendix: Resources

The intro promised you'd need half a dozen more books to actually get good at this. Here they are (rounding up), in
roughly the order I'd reach for them, followed by deeper dives on single topics.

**On communication itself:**

* [kind.engineering](https://kind.engineering) (Evan Smith) — how to be kind *and* honest at work: code reviews,
  feedback, one-to-ones. Free, short and developer-native, so start here.
* [Emotional Intelligence for Engineers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZU1B9LGjnAA) (April Wensel) — a conference
  talk making the case for empathy as an engineering skill.
* [*Simply Said*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/33232697-simply-said) (Jay Sullivan) — the general
  how-to-communicate book: plain language, focusing on the listener, structuring what you say.
* [*Nonviolent Communication*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/71730.Nonviolent_Communication) (Marshall
  Rosenberg) — the classic on saying hard things without starting a war. Much of the thinking behind
  [Hard conversations](#hard-conversations) traces back to it.
* [*Surrounded by Idiots*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/39101777-surrounded-by-idiots) (Thomas Erikson) — a
  four-colour model of how differently people want to be talked to. The science behind it is shaky, but as a working
  vocabulary for "adjust to the receiver" it does the job.
* [*How to Win Friends and Influence People*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/4865.How_to_Win_Friends_Influence_People)
  (Dale Carnegie) — the 1936 classic on making people feel heard. The examples show their age, but the mechanics
  still work.
* [*The Culture Map*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/22085568-the-culture-map) (Erin Meyer) — how bluntness,
  deadlines and decisions read across cultures. Already recommended in [Crossing cultures](#crossing-cultures), and
  it earns the second mention.
* [*Radical Candor*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/29939161-radical-candor) (Kim Scott) — feedback that is
  caring and direct at the same time. Written for managers, but the framework applies to peers just as well.
* [*Crucial Conversations*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/15014.Crucial_Conversations) (Joseph Grenny et al.)
  — what to do when stakes are high, opinions differ and emotions run strong. The full-length treatment of the
  [Hard conversations](#hard-conversations) part.

**Deep dives on single topics:**

* [The Guerrilla Guide to Interviewing](https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2006/10/25/the-guerrilla-guide-to-interviewing-version-30/)
  (Joel Spolsky) — the interviewer's side of the table. Old but still worth the twenty minutes.
* [*Software Estimation: Demystifying the Black Art*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/93891.Software_Estimation)
  (Steve McConnell) — a whole book on what [Providing estimates](#providing-estimates) squeezes into a page. Read it
  if estimates rule your life.
* [*TED Talks: The Official TED Guide to Public Speaking*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/41044212-ted-talks)
  (Chris Anderson) — for [Presenting](#presenting), from the man who runs TED.
* [*Demystifying Public Speaking*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/32784222-demystifying-public-speaking) (Lara
  Hogan) — the alternative for nervous engineers: short, practical and gentle.
* [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr) — a framework for structuring documentation, the "what to write" side that
  [Documentation](#documentation) leaves out.
* [Google's code review guidelines](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/) — battle-tested defaults for
  both sides of a review.
* [*On Writing Well*](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/53343.On_Writing_Well) (William Zinsser) — plain
  non-fiction writing; it sharpens everything from [Writing](#writing) to postmortems.
